title: Midterm: Lectures 1 to 3

cards.title: Learning goals 1 to 4
cards.body: The chapter has seven learning goals. Goal 1: obligations to global stakeholders (shareholders, workers, communities and governments, all at once). Goal 2: human rights abroad, where expectations for MNCs have risen sharply in recent decades. Goal 3: CSR and codes of ethics as strategy. Goal 4: practical guidance for a manager when ethical standards differ across cultures.
cards.example: Goal 3: CSR is a real competitive factor, not just good PR.

cards.title: Learning goals 5 to 7
cards.body: Goal 5: companies must give back to their host countries to keep their “social license to operate”. Goal 6: sustainability has to be built into long-term strategy, not treated as an afterthought. Goal 7: China is the comparative case study.
cards.example: China: huge opportunity, hard human-rights questions.

cards.title: Opening profile: Primark
cards.body: The lecture opens with Primark and the true cost of fast fashion. The slides show photos only. One photo shows garment workers in Bangladesh holding signs. The other shows protesters outside a Primark store holding signs. The slides give no further details.
cards.example: Signs: “I made your clothes”, “Primark's shame”, “Never again”.

cards.title: CSR and ethics
cards.body: CSR is a company regulating itself: going beyond the legal minimum, voluntarily. It means actively monitoring your own compliance with laws, ethics and social norms. Ethics is the decisions and interactions of individuals. CSR decisions are bigger: made at a higher level, and affecting far more people.
cards.example: 2003: the UN drafted its first CSR guidelines for multinational corporations.

cards.title: The CSR dilemma
cards.body: CSR weighs the benefit against the harm MNCs create, especially in developing countries. The big question is how much a firm should care about the social effects of its decisions. One extreme: profit is the MNC's only goal. The other extreme: MNCs should anticipate and solve social needs. Most real firms sit in between, and that position shifts under pressure.
cards.example: “We only owe you profit” versus “we should actively solve social problems”.

cards.title: Core CSR issues
cards.body: The core CSR issues are poverty, environment, consumer rights and worker safety. These issues are now mapped onto the UN's 17 SDGs. The SDGs come back later in the lecture, on slides 45 and 46.
cards.example: Four core issues: poverty, environment, consumer rights, worker safety.

cards.title: MNC stakeholders
cards.body: Home-country stakeholders: owners, employees, customers, unions, suppliers, strategic allies, distributors, society in general, community, economy, government. Host-country stakeholders: economy, community, employees, host government, consumers, suppliers, strategic allies, distributors. Global stakeholders: global interdependence and standard of living, global environment and ecology, sustainable resources, population's standard of living.
cards.example: Diagram: the MNC in the middle, home and host stakeholders around it, global stakeholders around both.

cards.title: International CSR is harder
cards.body: International CSR is harder than domestic CSR: more stakeholders, more conflicts of interest. Managers must weigh home-country rights against host-country rights, and the answer is rarely clean. Del Monte's pineapple farms in Kenya bring export earnings but take up scarce farmland.
cards.example: Pakistan soccer balls: pay a living wage and risk hunger for families who lose the work, or keep wages low and risk child labour.

cards.title: Global consensus or variation
cards.body: “Global Corporate Culture” is the idea that business norms are converging worldwide. In practice the US and Europe still diverge, rooted in different histories and philosophies. The US approach is clear, universal rules: “do business right” and treat everyone by the same standard. The EU approach is broader social aims: environment, shared values, relationships.
cards.example: The 2024 Forced Labour Regulation reflects the EU's tougher, systemic tradition.

cards.title: Dealing with confusion
cards.body: The slide gives three ways to deal with confusion about cross-cultural dilemmas. First, engage stakeholders (and sometimes NGOs) in a dialog. Second, establish principles and procedures for difficult issues. Third, adjust reward systems to reflect the company's commitment to CSR.
cards.example: Difficult issues named: labor standards for suppliers, environmental reporting, human rights.

cards.title: Three approaches to ethics
cards.body: The slide gives three approaches for a code of morality and ethics. Moral universalism: a moral standard accepted by all cultures. Ethnocentric approach: apply the morality of the home country, regardless of the host country's system of ethics. Ethical relativism: adopt the local moral code of whatever country the firm operates in.
cards.example: Moral universalism is marked “preferable”. Ethical relativism is marked “conflict”.

cards.title: Three industry codes
cards.body: Sweatshop Code of Conduct (Clinton-era, 1990s): bans forced labour and discrimination, sets minimum wage and safety rules. Responsible Business Alliance (formerly the Electronic Industry Code of Conduct): a whole industry self-regulating; bans child and forced labour and excessive overtime, requires supplier audits. Social Accountability 8000 (SA8000): an ISO-style, certifiable labour standard.
cards.example: Sweatshop Code: Nike, Reebok, Walmart, Liz Claiborne. RBA: HP, Dell, IBM, Intel and 12+ more. SA8000: Avon, Sainsbury's.

cards.title: UN Global Compact
cards.body: The UN Global Compact aims to mobilize a global movement of sustainable companies and stakeholders. It supports companies to do business responsibly by aligning strategies and operations with 10 Principles on four areas: human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. It also pushes action to advance the SDGs, with an emphasis on collaboration and innovation.
cards.example: 23,000+ business participants in 160+ countries (2025, 25th anniversary).

cards.title: Global Compact principles
cards.body: Slide 16 is titled “10 principles” but lists nine bullets. They are: respect of human rights; the right to collective bargaining; elimination of forced labour; abolition of child labour; elimination of discrimination in employment; a precautionary approach to environmental challenges; greater environmental responsibility; diffusion of environmentally friendly technologies; work against corruption in all its forms.
cards.example: Four areas from slide 15: human rights, labour, environment, anti-corruption.

cards.title: Getz's five codes
cards.body: Getz's integrated international codes of conduct combine five sources. One: International Chamber of Commerce Guidelines for International Investments. Two: The OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. Three: ILO Tripartite Declaration of Principles Concerning Multinational Enterprises and Social Policy. Four: UN Code of Conduct of Transnational Corporations. Five: UN Universal Declaration for Human Rights.
cards.example: Author to remember: Getz.

cards.title: Three areas of the codes
cards.body: The codes cover three areas. MNC and Host Governments: economic and development policies, law and regulations, political involvement. MNC and Public: technology transfer, environmental protection. MNC and Persons: consumer protection, employment practices, human rights.
cards.example: Slides 19 to 25 detail seven of the eight sub-areas. Human rights has no detail slide.

cards.title: Host government: economic policy
cards.body: Economic and development policies. Investments should conform to the host country's economic and social development. They should help resolve balance of payments and exchange rate difficulties, ensure local equity participation, and not dominate capital markets. Taxes are paid to host governments, the tax base is not modified, raw materials come from local sources, and profits are reinvested in host countries.
cards.example: Eight points in total, from local development to reinvesting profits.

cards.title: Host government: law and politics
cards.body: Law and regulations: the MNC obeys the laws of the country where it operates, respects its right to control natural resources and to regulate, uses international dispute settlement including arbitration, and resolves expropriation disputes under host-country law. Political involvement: no improper involvement in local politics, no bribes to any public servant, no interference in intergovernmental relations.
cards.example: Political involvement: should not pay bribes to any public servant.

cards.title: Public and consumers
cards.body: Technology transfer: cooperate with governments to build technological capacity of developing countries, develop technologies for local needs, do R&D with local resources and personnel. Environmental protection: respect host-country environmental law, cooperate with governments and IO on standards, supply information on environmental impacts. Consumer protection: respect consumer law, protect safety and health by disclosure, proper labelling and accurate advertising.
cards.example: Three areas here: technology transfer, environmental protection, consumer protection.

cards.title: Employment practices
cards.body: Employment practices: cooperate with governments to create jobs in particular localities; try to increase employment opportunities and standards in host countries; give advance notice of plant closures and mitigate effects; provide standards equal to or better than local ones; pay at minimum basic living wages; keep the highest safety and health standards and give adequate information about work-related hazards.
cards.example: Two anchors: advance notice of plant closures, basic living wages.

cards.title: Why China attracts business
cards.body: The case study is business in China (slide title: “Comparative Management in Focus: Business in China”). The slide lists four attractions: a skilled workforce, 1.4B consumers, an EV and green-tech hub, and the 2nd-largest economy.
cards.example: 1.4B consumers and the 2nd-largest economy.

cards.title: China: human rights issues
cards.body: The slide has two columns. Challenges: potentially rampant violation of workers' rights; repression of free speech; difficulty monitoring and correcting human rights violations. Issues in China, as named: Nike, Xinjiang cotton bans and forced-labour import laws, Shein, H&M, Apple. The slide does not pair each name with a challenge.
cards.example: Names on the slide: Nike, Shein, H&M, Apple.

cards.title: Business ethics varies
cards.body: International business ethics is the business conduct or morals of MNCs in their relationship with individuals and entities. Ethics vary based on the cultural value system in each country or society. So practices considered illegal in some countries are accepted ways of doing business in others.
cards.example: Slide 28: illegal in one country, an accepted way of doing business in another.

cards.title: Moral philosophy of societies
cards.body: Exhibit 2-3 comes from Robertson and Crittenden (2003). It is a flow. Economic ideology (capitalism versus socialism) and culture (Western versus Eastern) lead to a dominant moral philosophy. That leads to ethical or unethical societal norms, which lead to individual behavior. Three groups of moderators act on the flow.
cards.example: Macro: natural resources, GDP per capita, government form, stability. Societal: language, religion, traditions. Firm: culture, policies, profit motive.

cards.title: To bribe or not to bribe
cards.body: The slide gives three situations. Paying mail carriers in Mexico to prevent them from “losing” mail. Paying $100 to get a computer picked up, not left on a rainy dock. Gift-giving to bond social ties.
cards.example: Slide title: “To Bribe or NOT to Bribe?”

cards.title: Questionable payments
cards.body: Questionable payments are political payments, extortion, bribes or “grease money” to speed up routine transactions. In some cultures bribery is treated as normal, and gift-giving is common and expected. Key difference: gift-giving is open; bribery is secret and transactional. Bribery of officials is illegal everywhere, regardless of local custom.
cards.example: The dilemma: stick to your own standard and risk losing business, or match local practice and risk the law.

cards.title: FCPA and the OECD convention
cards.body: The FCPA (US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) bans bribing foreign officials to win business. Penalties include heavy fines and prison. 2025 update: Trump paused FCPA enforcement (Feb to Jun 2025); the DOJ reopened it in June 2025, refocused on bribery tied to cartels and organised crime. Even “universal” rules can shift with politics.
cards.example: OECD Anti-Bribery Convention: signed by 36+ countries, hard to enforce without a formal complaint.

cards.title: CPI: least corrupt
cards.body: The slide is titled Global Corruption Barometer (CPI). Its footnote says Transparency International's 2025 CPI, the Corruption Perceptions Index. Scores run 0 to 100, and a higher score means less corrupt. Least corrupt in 2025: Denmark 89, Finland 88, Singapore 84, New Zealand 81, Norway 81, Sweden 80, Switzerland 80, Netherlands 78, Germany 77.
cards.example: Denmark is at the top with 89.

cards.title: CPI: most corrupt and facts
cards.body: Most corrupt in 2025: South Sudan 8, Somalia 9, Venezuela 10, Syria 12, Yemen 13, Equatorial Guinea 13. In the 2025 CPI, 182 countries were scored 0 to 100. The global average fell to a record-low 42.
cards.example: Lithuania scores 65 (rank 28). The US scored 64 (rank 29, its lowest ever).

cards.title: Policies for ethical behaviour
cards.body: Four policies help MNCs deal with ethical behaviour: develop a worldwide code of ethics; build ethical policies into strategy development; plan regular assessment of the company's ethical posture; if ethical problems cannot be resolved, withdraw from that market. Questionable behavior can be a “slippery slope”.
cards.example: A small bribe, a matter of personal ethics, can over time become truly negligent and perhaps criminal.

cards.title: Criticisms 1 to 3
cards.body: Common criticisms of MNC subsidiary activities, part one. One: MNCs raise capital locally, which can push up interest rates for domestic firms. Two: subsidiaries are usually majority- or fully-owned by the parent, so host-country people have little real control. Three: MNCs reserve senior managerial and technical roles for expatriates, slowing local talent development.
cards.example: Criticism 3: senior roles go to expatriates.

cards.title: Criticisms 4 to 9
cards.body: Four: technology is not always adapted to local conditions. Five: R&D stays at headquarters, limiting technology transfer. Six: can fuel demand for luxury goods over essential goods. Seven: often enters by buying an existing firm. Eight: can dominate whole industries, raising demand for scarce resources and inflation. Nine: answers only to home-country shareholders and government.
cards.example: Criticism 9: not accountable to the host nation's own development plans.

cards.title: Benefits and costs to hosts
cards.body: Managing the subsidiary and host-country relationship goes beyond CSR. Benefits: outside capital, foreign-exchange earnings, technology, infrastructure development, new jobs, local management development. Costs: competition for capital, increased interest rates, inappropriate technology, development investment exceeding benefits, limited skills development, few managerial jobs for locals.
cards.example: “MNCs must learn to accommodate the needs of other organizations and countries.”

cards.title: Nationalism, protectionism, governmentalism
cards.body: Three host-country stances. Under nationalism, public opinion favours national goals and is against foreign influences. Under protectionism, the host partly or fully closes borders to withstand foreign products, using tariff and nontariff barriers. Under governmentalism, the government uses policy-setting to favour national interests, not market forces.
cards.example: Protectionism uses tariff and nontariff barriers.

cards.title: Exporting the risk
cards.body: Developed countries export growing volumes of hazardous waste and banned chemicals to developing ones. Monsanto (acquired by Bayer in 2018) sold pesticides abroad that were banned in the US. The twist: produce grown with those pesticides is often re-imported as food, so “exporting the risk” does not fully protect the exporting country.
cards.example: The slide: the US exports roughly 200 million lbs of pesticides a year that are banned for use at home.

cards.title: Industrial ecology
cards.body: Industrial ecology views an industrial system together with its surrounding environment, to optimise the total materials cycle from virgin material to ultimate disposal. To deal with ecological interdependence, strategic planning integrates three things: looking for alternative raw materials, developing new methods of recycling, and expanding use of by-products.
cards.example: Three steps: alternative raw materials, new recycling methods, more use of by-products.

cards.title: Sustainability and development
cards.body: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without compromising tomorrow's resources. Its three pillars, the “Triple Bottom Line”: Economic + Social + Environmental. It also includes future generations, biodiversity, human rights, transparency, education. Sustainable development became the main guiding principle after the Rio conference of 1992, and respects the limited capacity of an ecosystem to absorb human impact.
cards.example: Rio conference, 1992.

cards.title: Agenda 2030 and the SDGs
cards.body: In September 2015, 193 countries adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Its goal is balanced economic, social and environmental development that will “leave no one behind”. It has 17 SDGs with measurable targets. The slide adds a 2026 reality check: with 4 years left, fewer than 1 in 5 targets are on track.
cards.example: SDG examples: no poverty, zero hunger, climate action. The full list of 17 is in the glossary.

cards.title: Recommendations for MNCs
cards.body: For MNCs in developing countries: do no intentional harm (including ecosystem integrity and consumer safety); produce more good than harm; contribute to host-country development; respect employees' human rights; respect local culture and work with it if it does not violate ethical norms; pay a fair share of taxes; cooperate with local government on just background institutions.
cards.example: Seven recommendations in total.

cards.title: Final remarks
cards.body: Three closing points. One: managing interdependence means weighing ecological, economic and social impact together, not one after the other. Two: the core tension is low prices versus environmental and social responsibility. Three: there is no single global standard, because environmental and health policy still varies widely by country.
cards.example: Core tension: low prices versus environmental and social responsibility.

cards.title: Chapter learning goals
cards.body: The chapter sets six goals. Understand how culture affects international management, including communication and negotiations. Distinguish the major dimensions of cultural difference. See why managers need cultural intelligence in host countries. Recognize critical value differences. Build a working cultural profile of a society. Understand how culture and the Internet interact.
cards.example: Goal 5: a cultural profile is an aid to expected attitudes toward work, communication and negotiations.

cards.title: Opening profile: Saudi Arabia
cards.body: The lecture opens with Saudi Arabian culture. Saudi Arabia covers most of the Arabian peninsula. Its neighbours are all Arab and predominantly Islamic. Women outnumber men in universities and own 20 percent of all businesses. About 77 percent of the total workforce is still foreign-born.
cards.example: Women are now about 35 percent of the Saudi workforce, up from just 17 percent in 2017.

cards.title: Huntington: clash of civilizations
cards.body: S. P. Huntington argued that the main source of conflict in the new world will be cultural, not ideological or economic. Nation states stay powerful, but the main conflicts will be between nations and groups of different civilizations. The fault lines between civilizations will be the battle lines of the future.
cards.example: The map (s7) labels Western, Orthodox, Islamic, Sinic, Hindu, Japanese, Latin American and African, plus smaller areas such as Buddhist.

cards.title: What culture is
cards.body: Culture is acquired knowledge that people use to interpret experience and generate social behavior. It does three things. It forms values, it creates attitudes, and it influences behavior.
cards.example: Three effects of culture: forms values, creates attitudes, influences behavior.

cards.title: Six characteristics of culture
cards.body: Culture is learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned and adaptive. Learned means people acquire it from their society. Shared means members of a group hold it in common. Transgenerational means it passes from one generation to the next.
cards.example: The six words: learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned, adaptive.

cards.title: Values in culture
cards.body: Values are basic convictions that people have about what is right and wrong, good and bad, important and unimportant. People learn them from the culture in which they are educated, and they influence behavior. Differences in cultural values may result in varying management practices.
cards.example: Three pairs on the slide: right and wrong, good and bad, important and unimportant.

cards.title: Culture and organizations
cards.body: At the level of organizations, culture is a set of shared values, understandings, assumptions and goals. People learn it from earlier generations. Present members of a society impose it. It is passed on to succeeding generations.
cards.example: Three steps: learned from earlier generations, imposed by present members, passed on to succeeding generations.

cards.title: Schein's culture triangle
cards.body: Edgar Schein's model has three levels. Artefacts and symbols are visible: logos, architecture, structure, processes, corporate clothing. Espoused values are standards, values and rules of conduct, and how strategies and philosophies are made public. Basic underlying assumptions are deeply embedded, self-evident and unconscious, and hard to recognize from within.
cards.example: Problems could arise when managers' ideas are not in line with the basic assumptions of the organization.

cards.title: Schein's model on society
cards.body: Schein's model also works for a whole society. The top level is the explicit artifacts and products of the society. The middle level is the norms and values that guide the society. The deepest level is the implicit, basic assumptions that guide people's behavior.
cards.example: Organization level: artefacts, espoused values, assumptions. Society level: products, norms and values, implicit assumptions.

cards.title: The onion model
cards.body: Schein's model is also called the onion model. The outer layer is easy to adapt and change. The deeper the layer, the harder it is to adjust. Assumptions sit in the core and values around the core. Between artefacts and values there may be a layer of heroes: admired people who play or played an important role.
cards.example: Artefacts and symbols sit in the outer layers and can be changed most easily.

cards.title: Cultural sensitivity
cards.body: Cultural sensitivity, also called cultural empathy, is an awareness of and an honest caring about another individual's culture. The learning goals say managers need cultural intelligence to interact successfully in host countries.
cards.example: Two parts: awareness of the culture, and honest caring about it.

cards.title: Organizational culture
cards.body: Organizational culture exists within and interacts with societal culture. It varies a great deal from one organization, company, institution or group to another. It represents the expectations, norms and goals held in common by members of that group.
cards.example: It functions like societal culture, but varies a great deal within a single societal culture.

cards.title: The convergence debate
cards.body: How far culture affects organizational processes is a subject of debate. Some say convergence is making management styles more similar to one another. They name industrialization and worldwide coordination as the reasons. Convergence is the shifting of individual management styles to become similar.
cards.example: Reasons given for convergence: industrialization and worldwide coordination.

cards.title: Organizations respond to society
cards.body: Organizational culture is at least partly a function of societal culture and must respond to it. The airline KLM extended its travel benefits to any couple who formally registered as living together. McDonald's gives more training in Russia than in the US.
cards.example: McDonald's reason: Russians are less familiar with working within a capitalist system.

cards.title: Culture's effect on processes
cards.body: The slide compares US assumptions with alternatives. Individual influences future, or life is preordained: planning and scheduling. Environment is changeable, or people adjust to it: morale and productivity. Hard work leads to success, or wisdom and luck are also needed: motivation and rewards. Employment can be ended, or is for a lifetime: promotions and recruitment.
cards.example: Employment for a lifetime, instead of employment that can be ended, affects promotions and recruitment.

cards.title: Self-reference criterion
cards.body: The self-reference criterion is the subconscious reference point of one's own cultural values. Many people in the world understand and relate to others only in terms of their own cultures. The slide's printed example, worded unclearly, mentions Japanese workers who interrupt conversation with Americans when there are problems.
cards.example: Key word: subconscious. The reference point is your own culture's values.

cards.title: Parochialism and ethnocentrism
cards.body: Parochialism occurs when, for example, a Frenchman expects those from another country to fall automatically into patterns of behavior common in France. Ethnocentrism is the attitude of those who assume that their ways of doing things are best, no matter where or under what conditions they are applied.
cards.example: A Camay soap commercial (P&G, US) backfired in Japan; Japanese viewers saw the man's behavior as bad manners.

cards.title: Subcultures and stereotyping
cards.body: Many countries comprise diverse subcultures whose members conform only in varying degrees to the national character. Stereotyping here means a cultural profile that develops tentative expectations, some cultural context, as a backdrop to managing in a specific international setting.
cards.example: Canada is the slide's example of subcultures. Distinct ethnic groups in China have their own customs and dialects.

cards.title: Cultural subsystems 1 to 4
cards.body: Kinship guides family relationships: the nuclear family in the US, the extended family in some other countries. Education influences expectations of workers and choices about recruitment, staffing, training and leadership. The economic system influences sourcing, distribution, incentives and reparation of capital. The government and political system imposes constraints on organizations.
cards.example: Four of seven: kinship, education, economic system, government and political system.

cards.title: Cultural subsystems 5 to 7
cards.body: Religion commonly underlies moral and economic norms. A country's system of health affects employee productivity, expectations and attitudes toward physical fitness. Workers' attitudes about recreation can affect their work behavior and their perception of the role of work in their lives.
cards.example: Seven in total: kinship, education, economic, political, religion, health, recreation.

cards.title: Cultural values and profiles
cards.body: Values determine how individuals probably will act in given circumstances. They are communicated via the seven subsystems and passed down through generations. Contingency management requires managers to adapt to the local environment. Value dimensions and cultural profiles give only an approximation of national character.
cards.example: Americans tend to think of the Chinese as culturally homogenous, but ethnic groups in China differ.

lessons.title: Hall, Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck, Lewis, Gesteland, Schwartz

cards.title: Models of culture: the list
cards.body: Slide 27 lists attempts to assess cultural differences. Edward Hall, The silent language (1959). Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck (1961). Richard D. Lewis, When Cultures Collide (1996). Richard Gesteland (1996). Geert Hofstede (1997 edition). Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner, Riding the Waves of Culture (1997). S. Schwartz (2009). The GLOBE project (2007 book).
cards.example: Eight attempts: Hall, Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck, Lewis, Gesteland, Hofstede, Trompenaars, Schwartz, GLOBE.

cards.title: Hall: three big differences
cards.body: Edward T. Hall names the most important differences between cultures. First, proxemics: the amount of space people feel they must set between themselves and others, with high contact and low contact. Second, high context and low context. Third, polychronic versus monochronic time.
cards.example: Zones: intimate 0.45 m (1.5 ft), personal 1.2 m (4 ft), social 3.6 m (12 ft), public 7.6 m (25 ft).

cards.title: High and low context
cards.body: Low context: explicit messages, little attention to the status of the person, task oriented. High context: not just the message is important, relation oriented. From most high-context: Japanese, Arabic, Latin American, Italian, English, French, North American, Scandinavian (except Finland), German, Swiss-German.
cards.example: Japanese is most high-context on the slide. Swiss-German is least high-context.

cards.title: Monochronic people
cards.body: Monochronic people do one thing at a time and concentrate on the job. They take time commitments seriously and are committed to the job. They adhere religiously to plans. They worry about not disturbing others, and about privacy. They seldom borrow or lend. They are accustomed to short-term relationships.
cards.example: Opposite pair: monochronic people seldom borrow or lend; polychronic people borrow and lend often and easily.

cards.title: Polychronic people
cards.body: Polychronic people do many things at once and are highly distractible, subject to interruptions. They consider an objective to be achieved, if possible. They are committed to people and human relationships. They change plans often and easily. They are concerned with those closely related. They borrow and lend often and easily, and tend to build lifetime relationships.
cards.example: Monochronic: committed to the job. Polychronic: committed to people and human relationships.

cards.title: Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck 1 to 3
cards.body: Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck (1961) ask six questions. Nature of people: good (changeable or unchangeable), evil, or a mixture of good and evil. Relationship to nature: dominant, in harmony, or subjugation. Relationship to other people: lineal (hierarchical), collateral (collectivist), or individualist.
cards.example: Book: Variations in Value Orientations (Peterson, New York, 1961).

cards.title: Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck 4 to 6
cards.body: The other three questions. Modality of human activity: doing, being, or containing. Temporal focus of human activity: future, present, or past. Conception of space: private, public, or mixed.
cards.example: Time appears as the temporal focus: future, present or past.

cards.title: Lewis: linear-active
cards.body: Richard D. Lewis (When Cultures Collide) sorts cultures into three categories. Linear-active: talks half the time, does one thing at a time, plans ahead step by step, polite but direct, partly conceals feelings, confronts with logic, dislikes losing face, rarely interrupts, job-oriented, sticks to facts, truth before diplomacy.
cards.example: Triangle corner: Germany and Switzerland. Blue on the key: cold, factual, decisive planners.

cards.title: Lewis: multi-active
cards.body: Multi-active: talks most of the time, does several things at once, plans grand outline only, emotional, displays feelings, confronts emotionally, has good excuses, often interrupts, people-oriented, feelings before facts, flexible truth.
cards.example: Triangle corner: Hispanic America. Red on the key: warm, emotional, loquacious, impulsive.

cards.title: Lewis: reactive
cards.body: Reactive: listens most of the time, reacts to partner's action, looks at general principles, polite and indirect, conceals feelings, never confronts, must not lose face, does not interrupt, very people-oriented, statements are promises, diplomacy over truth.
cards.example: Triangle corner: Vietnam. Yellow on the key: courteous, amiable, accommodating, compromiser, good listener.

cards.title: Lewis triangle: countries
cards.body: Countries sit between the corners. Linear-active to multi-active side: U.S.A., Netherlands and Norway, Australia and Denmark, Belgium, France, Russia, Italy, Spain and Portugal. Multi-active to reactive side: Africans, Arabs, Iran and Turkey, India, Indonesia and Philippines, Korea, China. Base: U.K., Sweden, Finland, Canada, Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan.
cards.example: Canada sits in the middle of the base, between linear-active and reactive.

cards.title: Gesteland's cultural groups
cards.body: Richard Gesteland sorts cultures into Cultural Groups (A-G). He uses four features: deal focus or relationship focus, formal or unformal, polychronic or monochronic, and reserved or expressive. His book is Cross-cultural business behaviour (Copenhagen Business School Press).
cards.example: Four pairs: deal/relationship, formal/unformal, polychronic/monochronic, reserved/expressive.

cards.title: Schwartz: seven value types
cards.body: Shalom H. Schwartz's model is a circle of seven value types. Harmony: unity with nature, world at peace. Embeddedness: social order, obedience, respect for tradition. Hierarchy: authority, humble. Mastery: ambition, daring. Affective autonomy: pleasure, exciting life. Intellectual autonomy: broadmindedness, curiosity. Egalitarianism: social justice, equality.
cards.example: Source: Culture matters: National value cultures, sources and consequences (2009).

cards.title: Schwartz: results by region
cards.body: South American cultures clustered in the middle of the model. English speaking countries highly valued Mastery, with higher values on Hierarchy than on Egalitarianism. Western Europe was mainly around Egalitarianism and Intellectual Autonomy. Eastern Europe also favoured Egalitarianism, a little more towards Embeddedness. In the Middle East and most of Asia, Embeddedness and Hierarchy dominated.
cards.example: Middle East and most of Asia: Embeddedness and Hierarchy dominate.

cards.title: Hofstede and the IBM research
cards.body: Geert Hofstede developed a theory to measure cultural differences. His problem was how to quantify culture. He defined culture in six dimensions, based on research at IBM: power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term orientation, indulgence. The research covered 116,000 people in 50 countries, all in one firm, so read the results with caution.
cards.example: He found four dimensions first. Long-term orientation and indulgence were added later.

cards.title: Power distance
cards.body: Power distance is a society's acceptance of unequal power distribution. In high power distance cultures, formal authority and hierarchy are very respected, so leadership tends to be autocratic and centralized. In low power distance cultures, superiors and subordinates are more likely to see one another as equals, leading to more cooperation.
cards.example: Older table (s48): Malaysia 100 is first; Denmark 18 and Israel 13 are near the bottom.

cards.title: Uncertainty avoidance
cards.body: Uncertainty avoidance is the extent to which people feel threatened by ambiguous situations. High: strict laws, closely followed procedures, low-risk decisions, non-aggressive employees, lifetime employment common. Low: more comfortable with ambiguity, less formal and structured activities, managers take more risks, employees have more job mobility.
cards.example: Older table (s49): Greece 100 and Portugal 99 are high; Singapore 8 is the lowest listed.

cards.title: Individualism and collectivism
cards.body: Individualism is the tendency to look after yourself and your immediate family only and to neglect the needs of society. Democracy, individual initiative and achievement are valued. Collectivism entails tight social frameworks, emotional dependence on the organization and strong belief in group decisions. Higher individualism goes with higher GNPs and freer political systems.
cards.example: Older table (s52): US 90 is first, UK 89 third; Colombia 13 is the lowest listed.

cards.title: Masculinity and femininity
cards.body: Masculinity is the degree to which traditionally masculine values prevail: assertiveness, materialism, lack of concern for others. Femininity emphasizes concern for others, relationships and quality of life. More feminine cultures tend to have less work-family conflict, less job stress, more women in high-level jobs and a reduced need for assertiveness.
cards.example: Older table (s53): Japan 95 is first; Norway 8 is the lowest listed.

cards.title: Long-term orientation
cards.body: Every society keeps some links with its past while dealing with the present and future. Societies prioritise these goals differently. Low scorers are normative: they prefer time-honoured traditions and norms and view societal change with suspicion. High scorers are pragmatic: they encourage modern education to prepare for the future.
cards.example: Low score: normative, suspicious of change. High score: pragmatic, modern education.

cards.title: Indulgence and restraint
cards.body: Indulgence is defined as the extent to which people try to control their desires and impulses, based on the way they were raised. Relatively weak control is called Indulgence. Relatively strong control is called Restraint. Cultures can be described as Indulgent or Restrained.
cards.example: Weak control of desires: Indulgence. Strong control: Restraint.

cards.title: Older tables: PDI and UAI
cards.body: Slides 48 to 56 use older scores. Power distance (PDI): Malaysia 100, Arab countries 80, Japan 54, UK 35, Denmark 18, Israel 13; Lithuania 42 is written beside Jamaica. Uncertainty avoidance (UAI): Greece 100, Japan 92, Germany 65 (Lithuania 65 beside it), USA 46, Sweden 29, Singapore 8. China 30 is in brackets by Sweden.
cards.example: Lithuania's PDI 42 and UAI 65 match the newer chart on slide 58.

cards.title: Older tables: IDV and MAS
cards.body: Individualism (IDV): US 90, UK 89, Canada 80, Japan 46, China 20, Colombia 13; Lithuania 60 is written beside Finland. Masculinity (MAS): Japan 95, Austria 79, China 66, US 62, Denmark 16, Norway 8; Lithuania is printed as -19 beside Denmark. The true score on the newer chart is 19.
cards.example: Lithuania on the newer chart: individualism 60 and masculinity 19.

cards.title: Older table: long-term orientation
cards.body: The LTO table has older scores: China 100, Hong Kong 96, Taiwan 87, Japan 80 (Lithuania 82 beside it), South Korea 75, Germany 31, US 29, UK 25, Pakistan 00. Do not mix it with the newer chart on slide 58, where China is 87, Japan 88, Lithuania 82 and US 26.
cards.example: Use the newer chart (s58) for the China, Japan, Lithuania, US comparison.

cards.title: The four-country chart
cards.body: The Hofstede Insights chart compares China, Japan, Lithuania and US. Power distance: 80, 54, 42, 40. Individualism: 20, 46, 60, 91. Masculinity: 66, 95, 19, 62. Uncertainty avoidance: 30, 92, 65, 46. Long-term orientation: 87, 88, 82, 26. Indulgence: 24, 42, 16, 68.
cards.example: Read each list in the order China, Japan, Lithuania, US. Slide 57 is only a world map of indulgence.

cards.title: Trompenaars: seven dimensions
cards.body: Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner (Riding the Waves of Culture, 1997) give seven dimensions or dilemmas. Universalism vs particularism: obligations. Neutral vs emotional: emotions in relationship. Specific vs diffuse: privacy in relationship. Achievement vs ascription: source of power and status. Sequential vs synchronic. Internal vs external control. Individualism vs collectivism (communitarianism).
cards.example: Seven dimensions; the first four come with a short label (obligations, emotions, privacy, status).

cards.title: Obligation and emotion
cards.body: Universalistic cultures apply rules and systems objectively, without consideration of individual circumstances. Particularistic cultures put more emphasis on relationships and apply rules more subjectively. Affective or emotional cultures tend to express emotions openly, whereas neutral cultures do not.
cards.example: Obligations are measured as universalism vs particularism.

cards.title: Privacy, power and status
cards.body: People in specific cultures compartmentalize their work and private lives, and they are more open and direct. In diffuse cultures work spills over into personal relationships. In achievement-oriented cultures personal achievement is the source of status and influence. In ascription-oriented cultures status and influence come from society: class, age, gender, etc.
cards.example: Ascription: class, age and gender give status. Achievement: your own results do.

cards.title: Trompenaars: country rows
cards.body: Obligation, universalistic to particularistic: US, GER, SWE, UK, IT, FRA, JPN, SPA, SIN. Privacy in relationship, specific to diffuse: UK, US, FRA, GER, ITA, JPN, SWE, SPA, CHI. The rows for emotional orientation and source of power and status carry a copy-error label, so skip them.
cards.example: Left ends: US (universalistic) and UK (specific). Right ends: SIN (particularistic) and CHI (diffuse).

cards.title: The GLOBE project
cards.body: GLOBE is the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness Research Program. Robert J. House (Wharton) founded it in 1991. It uses questionnaires to create cultural dimensions and assess average values per country. It focuses on leadership behavior, is more in-depth, and separates desired from as-is preferences and organizational from societal values.
cards.example: Founded 1991 by Robert J. House (Wharton).

cards.title: GLOBE's nine dimensions
cards.body: The nine dimensions: uncertainty avoidance; power distance; collectivism I, social collectivism; collectivism II, in-group collectivism; gender egalitarianism; assertiveness; future orientation; performance orientation; humane orientation.
cards.example: The s71 table calls two of them collectivism/societal and gender differentiation.

cards.title: GLOBE and Hofstede
cards.body: GLOBE results correspond generally with those of Hofstede and Trompenaars. GLOBE differs from Hofstede because many more researchers with varied perspectives were involved, while Hofstede worked alone. GLOBE studied many companies, Hofstede only IBM. GLOBE gives a current overview of general stereotypes that can be analyzed further.
cards.example: Slides 67-68 add Hofstede codes: assertiveness (INDV), performance orientation (MAS), future orientation (LTO), humane orientation (FEM).

cards.title: Assertiveness and performance
cards.body: Assertiveness is how much people are expected to be tough, confrontational and competitive versus modest and tender. Low assertiveness countries have sympathy for the weak and stress loyalty and solidarity. Performance orientation is the importance of performance improvement and excellence. Low performance orientation countries put priority on tradition, loyalty, family and background, and associate competition with defeat.
cards.example: Low assertiveness: Sweden, New Zealand. Low performance orientation: Russia, Argentina.

cards.title: Future and humane orientation
cards.body: Future orientation is the level of importance a society attaches to future oriented behaviors such as planning and investing in the future. Humane orientation is the extent to which a society encourages and rewards people for being fair, altruistic, generous, caring and kind.
cards.example: Low future orientation: Russia, Argentina. Low humane orientation: Germany, Spain.

cards.title: GLOBE country results
cards.body: Slide 71 lists highest and lowest countries per dimension. Power distance: highest Russia and Spain, lowest Denmark and Netherlands. Uncertainty avoidance: highest Austria and Denmark, lowest Russia and Hungary. Collectivism/societal: highest Denmark and Singapore, lowest Greece and Hungary. In-group collectivism: highest Egypt and China, lowest Denmark and Netherlands. Gender differentiation: highest South Korea and Egypt, lowest Sweden and Denmark.
cards.example: Slides 69-70 and 71 disagree on some high lists, so trust the low lists on the assertiveness, performance and future cards.

cards.title: The ten GLOBE clusters
cards.body: The ten clusters are Anglo, Latin America, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Sub-Sahara Africa, Arab, Southern Asia and Confucian Asia. The slide is Exhibit 3-4, Geographic Culture Clusters. The next two cards list the countries as the slide shows them.
cards.example: Source: GLOBE data, Gupta, Hanges and Dorfman (2002).

cards.title: Cluster members, part 1
cards.body: Anglo: Australia, Canada, England, Ireland, New Zealand, South Africa, United States. Latin America: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Venezuela. Latin Europe: France, Israel, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland (French speaking). Eastern Europe: Albania, Georgia, Greece, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Poland, Russia, Slovenia.
cards.example: Israel sits in Latin Europe on this slide, and Greece and Russia in Eastern Europe.

cards.title: Cluster members, part 2
cards.body: Germanic Europe: Austria, Germany, Netherlands, Switzerland (German speaking). Nordic Europe: Denmark, Finland, Sweden. Sub-Sahara Africa: Nigeria, Zambia, Malawi, South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe (Black spots). Arab: Egypt, Kuwait, Morocco, Qatar, Turkey. Southern Asia: India, Indonesia, Iran, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand. Confucian Asia: China, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea.
cards.example: Turkey is in the Arab cluster. Japan is in Confucian Asia.

cards.title: Radar chart and overlapping models
cards.body: Slide 72 compares managerial perspectives in the US and Brazil on a radar chart, to show GLOBE can compare country profiles. Slide 74 shows the six models overlap on themes: power and status, group and individuals, relationship with environment, time, individual and social control, and other. Time appears in five of the six models.
cards.example: GLOBE has the most dimensions on relationship with environment (3).

lessons.title: Values in practice and the three cases

cards.title: Four critical value differences
cards.body: Four operational value differences matter for managers. Time: differences in temporal values. Change: control and pace of change. Material factors: physical goods and status symbols versus aesthetics and the spiritual side. Individualism: me or I versus we.
cards.example: Four items: time, change, material factors, individualism.

cards.title: Time and change
cards.body: To Americans, time is money and schedules are strictly kept. In Latin America the word for tomorrow means sometime in the future. Western people generally believe an individual can control the future and manipulate events. Many non-Western societies believe in destiny or the will of their God, and tend to be passive and hostile toward change.
cards.example: A Chinese worker may read a change to power machinery as dissatisfaction with his father's way of life.

cards.title: Material focus and individualism
cards.body: Americans tend to value physical goods and status symbols. Many non-Westerners worship nature as their religious belief and value the aesthetic and spiritual side instead. In the US, individual achievement takes precedence, with a focus on I. In countries like China there is more emphasis on conformity and cooperation.
cards.example: US: focus on I. China: conformity and cooperation.

cards.title: The Internet and culture
cards.body: 98 percent of Korean homes have high-speed Internet service. Technology is changing culture, especially associations, education and the economy. Culture also changes how technology is used. The US collects a great deal of consumer information. In Sweden and many other European countries the government closely monitors the use and sharing of consumer data.
cards.example: The Swedish airline example shows privacy protection and suggests some degree of uncertainty avoidance.

cards.title: Japan: comparative management
cards.body: Japan: wa, meaning peace and harmony. A mix of authoritarian and humanism in the workplace. Emphasis on participative management, consensus and duty. Open expression and conflict are discouraged.
cards.example: Wa links to the Tom Forrest case: open conflict in a meeting breaks harmony.

cards.title: Germany: comparative management
cards.body: Germany: preference for rules and order, and privacy. Dislike of inefficiency and tardiness. Assertive, but not aggressive. Organizations are centralized but still favor consensus decision making.
cards.example: Dislike of inefficiency and tardiness fits the Fred Wagner case in Frankfurt.

cards.title: South Korea: comparative management
cards.body: South Korea: respect for family, authority, formality and class. People are demonstrative, friendly, aggressive and hard-working. Connections are vital for business, and most contracts are oral. Honest criticism is rare.
cards.example: Most contracts are oral; connections are vital.

cards.title: Latin America: comparative management
cards.body: Latin America is not homogenous, but has common similarities. It is being-oriented compared with doing-oriented. Work and private lives are more closely integrated. It is very important to maintain harmony and save face.
cards.example: Harmony and saving face are very important; work and private lives are closely integrated.

cards.title: Saudi Arabia: management style
cards.body: The slide links three roots to three styles. Tribalism leads to paternalism and nepotism. Close friendships lead to person-orientation and Theory Y. Honor and shame lead to conflict avoidance and positive reinforcement.
cards.example: Honor and shame lead to conflict avoidance and positive reinforcement.

cards.title: Chinese family business
cards.body: Small, family businesses predominate. Guanxi connections matter. People are put ahead of business. Organizations do not include middle management.
cards.example: Four features: family businesses, guanxi, people before business, no middle management.

cards.title: The three cases
cards.body: Three cases ask what went wrong. Bill Nugent waited for a Saudi official and met small talk. Tom Forrest defended a plan in a Japanese meeting and the joint venture ended. Fred Wagner opened a Frankfurt presentation with humorous anecdotes and lost the distributor. Link each to the culture's slide concepts.
cards.example: Questions on the slides: how might you help Bill; how could you help Tom; what went wrong for Fred.

cards.title: Five learning goals
cards.body: The lecture has five goals. Recognize the cultural variables in the communication process and what causes 'noise'. Be aware of differences in non-verbal behaviors, context and attitudes. Understand Western-Arab communications. Be aware of the impact of IT and AI on cross-border communications. Learn how to manage cross-cultural communications.
cards.example: Goal 1 asks what factors can cause 'noise' in the communication process.

cards.title: Opening profile: Google
cards.body: Google Street View was frozen in Germany for 12 years (2011 to 2023) after about 244,000 households asked for their homes to be blurred. EU regulators (now the European Data Protection Board, under GDPR) keep challenging US tech data practices. The slide says there is a big difference in the culture of privacy between the US and Europe.
cards.example: Meta was fined 1.2 billion euros in 2023. TikTok was fined 530 million euros in 2025.

cards.title: Why communication matters
cards.body: The opening profile shows that communication is a critical factor in cross-cultural management issues. This is true most of all for interpersonal issues. The slide names four: motivation, leadership, group interactions and negotiation.
cards.example: The case is titled Google's Internet Communication clash.

cards.title: The communication process
cards.body: Exhibit 4-1 has three parts. The sender encodes meaning, the medium carries the message, and the receiver decodes the meaning. Noise acts on all three parts. Culture is the source that feeds the noise. Feedback runs from the receiver back to the sender.
cards.example: Sender, medium, receiver: noise on all three, feedback back to the sender.

cards.title: Cultural noise
cards.body: Intercultural communication occurs when a member of one culture sends a message to a member of another culture. The message holds the meaning the encoder intended. But the decoder's culture becomes part of the meaning when he or she interprets it.
cards.example: The decoder's culture ends up becoming part of the meaning.

cards.title: Attribution
cards.body: Attribution is the process in which people look for an explanation of another person's behavior. When someone does not understand another, he or she usually blames the confusion on the other's 'stupidity or craziness'. In the Greek case, each side explains the same behavior through its own culture.
cards.example: Greek says 'I don't know. How long should it take?' and the American thinks: He refuses to take responsibility.

cards.title: Trust and effective communication
cards.body: Effective communication depends on informal understandings among the parties, based on the trust developed between them. When trust exists, there is implicit understanding, cultural differences may be overlooked, and problems are dealt with more easily. The meaning of trust and how it is developed vary across societies. Some cultures have a greater propensity to trust.
cards.example: Trust creates implicit understanding inside communication.

cards.title: World Values Survey on trust
cards.body: The World Values Survey (WVS) studied 90,000 people in 45 societies. Nordic countries rated highest on believing that most people can be trusted. Brazil, Turkey, Romania, Slovenia and Latvia had the lowest trust in people. Business can rest on long-standing or on arm's length relationships.
cards.example: High propensity to trust (s10): Nordic countries, China, Canada, United States, Britain. Low: Brazil, Turkey, Romania, Slovenia and Latvia.

cards.title: Three guidelines to build trust
cards.body: The slide gives three guidelines for cultivating trust. Create a clear and calculated basis for mutual benefit. Improve predictability by striving to resolve conflicts and keeping communication open. Develop mutual bonding through regular socializing and friendly contacts.
cards.example: Mutual bonding comes from regular socializing and friendly contacts.

cards.title: GLOBE and communication style
cards.body: GLOBE shows which style fits which culture. High performance orientation (US, Switzerland, Germany): direct, explicit, objective information. Low performance orientation (Russia, Greece, Portugal): more indirect approach. Low assertiveness (Sweden, Nordic countries): friendly, two-way discourse. High humane orientation (Ireland, Indonesia, Philippines): avoid conflict, be supportive.
cards.example: Sweden is the low-assertiveness example on s11. Ireland is the high humane orientation example.

cards.title: The list of cultural variables
cards.body: Cultural variables affect communication via a person's perceptions. The list: attitudes, social organization, thought patterns, roles, language (spoken and written), non verbal communication, and time. Non verbal communication covers kinesic behavior, paralanguage, proxemics and object language. The effects of these variables are interdependent.
cards.example: The effects are interdependent: one variable cannot be read alone.

cards.title: Attitudes and stereotyping
cards.body: Attitudes underlie our behavior, communication and interpretation. Ethnocentric attitudes are a particular source of noise. Stereotyping occurs when a person assumes that every member of a society or subculture has the same characteristics. Astute managers deal with people as individuals.
cards.example: The s14 picture for attitudes shows stereotyping.

cards.title: Social organization
cards.body: The kinds of social organizations we belong to can influence our perceptions. Examples of social organizations are one's nation, tribe, religious sect or profession.
cards.example: The s14 picture example is the United Auto Workers (UAW).

cards.title: Thought patterns
cards.body: The logical progression of reasoning varies widely across cultures. We cannot assume others use the same reasoning processes.
cards.example: A Canadian in Thailand assumed double lines on the road meant 'no passing', just as in Canada.

cards.title: Roles
cards.body: Cultures differ in what they consider the role of a manager. They also differ on who should make decisions and who has responsibility for what.
cards.example: The s16 picture for roles reads: decision making and responsibility.

cards.title: Language problems
cards.body: When two people do not share a language, problems come from not understanding local idioms, failing to understand body language, or poor translation. Even where people share a language, problems can arise. Managers often deal with workforces that speak a variety of languages, even within a single country.
cards.example: Cause named on the slide: increasing diversity.

cards.title: Politeness and 'yes'
cards.body: When many Asians say 'yes', it often means only that they have heard you and are too polite to disagree. Politeness and a desire to say only what the listener wants to hear create noise in the communication process in much of the world.
cards.example: The s16 picture is titled: when 'yes' doesn't mean 'yes'.

cards.title: Language carries culture
cards.body: Britain and the US are two nations separated by a common language. Language also conveys cultural and social understanding from one generation to another. The slide's examples: 6000 Arabic words for camels and their parts, and 50 or more classifications of snow used by Inuit peoples. Sometimes how something is said matters more than what is said.
cards.example: Inuit peoples of Canada and Greenland: 50 or more classifications of snow.

cards.title: Translation problems
cards.body: Translation can be problematic as well. The slide's example is Pepsi. Come Alive with Pepsi was translated into German as Come out of the grave.
cards.example: The s16 picture shows 'come out of the grave with Pepsi'.

cards.title: Expressive and instrumental
cards.body: Expressive communicators make communication personal by showing emotions openly or using emotional appeals to persuade. Instrumental communicators put emphasis on the content of the communication, not on personal expression.
cards.example: Expressive: Russia, Hungary, Poland. Instrumental: Slovenia, Lithuania, Czech Republic.

cards.title: Nonverbal communication
cards.body: Nonverbal communication is behavior that communicates without words, though it is often accompanied by words. Nonverbal cues are often said to carry 65-93% of interpreted meaning (a debated estimate). Minor variations in body language, speech rhythms and punctuality often cause mistrust and misperception among cross-cultural parties.
cards.example: The slide quotes: 'A picture is worth a thousand words.'

cards.title: Four media of nonverbal
cards.body: Kinesic behavior is communication through body movements. Proxemics is the influence of proximity and space on communication, both personal space and office layout. Paralanguage is how something is said rather than the content. Object language (material culture) is communication through material artifacts.
cards.example: Oculesics is the slide's example of kinesic behavior.

cards.title: Proxemics and contact
cards.body: High-contact cultures stand close, touch a great deal and want a 'close' sensory involvement: South America, Arabs, South Europe. Low-contact cultures have a 'distant' style of body language: North America, Asia, North Europe. Japanese are less haptic (touching) and traditionally bow.
cards.example: Handshakes are common with foreigners, says the slide, although Japanese traditionally bow.

cards.title: Space, power and climate
cards.body: Space communicates power in the US and Germany. French executives show their central position by working in the middle of subordinates. Cooler climates and individualistic cultures: low-contact, low context, monochronic, linear active. Warmer climates and collectivistic cultures: high-contact, high context, polychronic, multi active.
cards.example: US executives may have large, private corner offices.

cards.title: Paralanguage and silence
cards.body: Paralanguage is how something is said, not the content. It includes rate of speech, tone and inflection of voice, other noises, laughing, yawning and silence. The Chinese tend to spend about 30 seconds thinking before they speak. Americans are comfortable with only 10 to 15 seconds of silence.
cards.example: Americans break the silence and offend the Chinese by interrupting his or her chain of thoughts.

cards.title: Three gesture pictures
cards.body: Slides 22 to 24 show three pictures: sticking out the tongue, widening of the eyes, and scratching ears and cheeks. The slides do not print the meanings. The classic reading for Chinese culture, not printed on the slide: tongue means surprise, wide eyes mean anger (politely expressed), scratching ears and cheeks means happiness.
cards.example: Classic reading, not on the slide: scratching ears and cheeks shows happiness.

cards.title: Monochronic and polychronic
cards.body: Monochronic cultures (Switzerland, Germany, United States): time is linear and is spent, saved, made up or wasted. People do one thing at a time and are used to short-term relationships. Polychronic cultures (Latin Americans, Arabs): time is nonlinear, many things happen at once, and people matter more than material things.
cards.example: Polychronic people may change plans often, hold open meetings and move around.

cards.title: Forms of nonverbal communication
cards.body: The slide lists eleven forms: facial expression; body posture; gestures with hands, arms, head; interpersonal distance (proxemics); touching and body contact; eye contact; clothing, cosmetics, hairstyle, jewelry; paralanguage (voice pitch, rate of speech, silence); color symbolism; attitude towards time and its use; food symbolism and social use of meals.
cards.example: Paralanguage and proxemics appear here as forms, in brackets.

cards.title: High and low context
cards.body: Context incorporates many cultural variables and affects the meaning of an interaction. High-context cultures (Asia, Middle East, Africa, Mediterranean): thoughts are not explicit, you read between the lines, style is indirect. Low-context cultures (Germany, Switzerland, US, Scandinavia): media are explicit, thoughts are put in words, style is straight.
cards.example: Germans expect detailed information before a decision. Arabs base decisions more on knowledge of the people involved.

cards.title: The context chart
cards.body: Exhibit 4-4 (based on Hall and Hall, 1990, and Rosch, 1987) runs from high context (implicit) to low context (explicit). The order: Japan, Middle East, Latin America, Africa, Mediterranean, England, France, North America, Scandinavia, Germany, Switzerland.
cards.example: Japan is at the high-context end. Switzerland is at the low-context end.

lessons.title: Asians, Arabs, channels and good practice

cards.title: Poker face and silence
cards.body: Americans put more emphasis on talking, and Asians more on listening. So Asian speakers send subtle cues, and the 'poker face' and 'idiotic smile' seem to Americans to conceal real feelings. To Americans silence is discontinuity. To Asians it is part of communication. Asians may find Americans overly talkative.
cards.example: Slide s32 sets the 'Oriental poker face' against the 'American mask of confidence'.

cards.title: Arab communication style
cards.body: Arabs use loud speech for dramatic effect. Communication is built on friendship, honor and hospitality. Arabs are high-contact communicators, and time is the key in the communication process. Arab culture is one of emotional extremes, shown in flowery language with many adjectives and words for exaggeration.
cards.example: The distance Americans prefer can make them seem suspicious and cold to Arabs.

cards.title: Arabs: business and time
cards.body: Arabs tend to do business with people, not with the organization. Protect the honor of others, do not decline hospitality, expect talk to move from social to business topics and back, and do not criticize in front of others. Arabs are polychronic and believe something happens only if Allah wills it.
cards.example: So placing deadlines on activities is inappropriate, and many interruptions should be expected.

cards.title: Suggestions for Arab business
cards.body: Five suggestions. Be patient: take the time needed to build relationship and trust. Relationships matter more than the task at hand. Avoid expressing doubts and criticism when others are present. Adapt to the norms of body language. Expect many interruptions in meetings, delays in schedules and changes in plans.
cards.example: Relationships matter more than the task at hand.

cards.title: Communication channels
cards.body: Channel variables matter for understanding the message: information systems, speed of information flow and use, and informal sources. In the US managers delegate, so information flows from staff to manager. In South America decision-making is centralized, so information flows from the manager downward. Japanese ringi systems decide by consensus.
cards.example: High-context: information spreads very rapidly. Low-context: it is focused and controlled and does not flow as freely.

cards.title: Japan versus the US
cards.body: Americans have a wide public self and give open access to informal sources. The Japanese keep a strong barrier between public and private selves. Japanese ningensei stresses saving and giving face, reciprocity and an underlying distrust of words. Americans are explicit, direct, task oriented and confrontational (adversarial).
cards.example: Americans like email, Slack, Teams. The French prefer slower written media, with several exchanges of letters.

cards.title: IT: going global, acting local
cards.body: Global reach does not necessarily mean global business. The Web is interpersonal but may require greater cultural sensitivity. Technology makes it easy to reach markets, yet companies must adapt e-commerce to local idiosyncrasies. The impersonal web must be adapted to local cultures to build relationships and customer loyalty.
cards.example: English is used on ~50% of websites, yet only about 1 in 4 internet users speaks it.

cards.title: Five steps to manage
cards.body: One: develop cultural sensitivity, anticipate the receiver's meaning. Two: careful encoding, use words, pictures and gestures, avoid slang and idioms. Three: selective transmission, build relationships, face-to-face if possible. Four: careful decoding of feedback, ask multiple parties. Five: follow-up actions, through action and inaction.
cards.example: Without face-to-face, phone calls and teleconferencing may beat email. Contracts are hard: cultures differ on what a contract is.

cards.title: Openness and resilience
cards.body: Facilitating intercultural communication needs openness and resilience. Openness: open-mindedness, tolerance for ambiguity, extrovertedness. Resilience: internal locus of control, persistence, tolerance for ambiguity, resourcefulness. The three aspects of adaptive change: increased functional fitness, psychological health, intercultural identity.
cards.example: Tolerance for ambiguity appears under both openness and resilience.

cards.title: Seven effective behaviors
cards.body: Behaviors associated with intercultural communication effectiveness: respect, interactive posture, orientation to knowledge, empathy, interaction management, tolerance for ambiguity, and other-oriented role behavior.
cards.example: Tolerance for ambiguity is also on the s44 lists of openness and resilience.

glossary.meaning: Corporate social responsibility: a company regulating itself voluntarily, going beyond the legal minimum, and actively monitoring its own compliance with laws, ethics and social norms.
The decisions and interactions of individuals. CSR decisions are bigger: made at a higher level and affecting far more people.
What a company keeps by giving back to its host countries (learning goal 5).
A moral standard accepted by all cultures. The slide marks it “preferable”.
Applying the morality used in the home country, regardless of the host country's system of ethics.
Adopting the local moral code of whatever country the firm operates in. The slide marks it “conflict”.
Where governments have not agreed on binding global rules, industry steps in with voluntary but reputation-critical codes. Examples: Sweatshop Code of Conduct, Responsible Business Alliance, SA8000.
Macro-level: natural resources, GDP per capita, form of government, political stability. Societal: language, religion, historic traditions. Firm-specific: corporate culture, policies, profit motive.
Political payments, extortion, bribes, or “grease money” to speed up routine transactions.
US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Bans bribing foreign officials to win business. Penalties include heavy fines and prison.
Transparency International's score from 0 to 100; a higher score means less corrupt. The slide titles it Global Corruption Barometer.

Nationalism: public opinion favours national goals. Protectionism: partial or full closing of borders with tariff and nontariff barriers. Governmentalism: government policy favours national interests, not market forces.
Viewing an industrial system together with its environment, to optimise the total materials cycle from virgin material to ultimate disposal.
The three pillars of sustainability: Economic + Social + Environmental.
Development that meets the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
1 No poverty, 2 Zero hunger, 3 Good health and well-being, 4 Quality education, 5 Gender equality, 6 Clean water and sanitation.

7 Affordable and clean energy, 8 Decent work and economic growth, 9 Industry, innovation and infrastructure, 10 Reduced inequalities, 11 Sustainable cities and communities, 12 Responsible consumption and production.
13 Climate action, 14 Life below water, 15 Life on land, 16 Peace, justice and strong institutions, 17 Partnerships for the goals.
Acquired knowledge that people use to interpret experience and generate social behavior. It forms values, creates attitudes and influences behavior.
Culture is learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned and adaptive.
Basic convictions about right and wrong, good and bad, important and unimportant. Learned from the culture where a person is educated, and they influence behavior.
Artefacts and symbols (visible, outer), espoused values (middle), basic underlying assumptions (deepest, unconscious, hard to recognize from within). Also called the onion model.
Also cultural empathy: an awareness of and an honest caring about another individual's culture.
The shifting of individual management styles to become similar to one another, said to come from industrialization and worldwide coordination.
The subconscious reference point of one's own cultural values. People understand others only in terms of their own cultures.
Expecting people from another country to fall automatically into patterns of behavior common in your own country, as a Frenchman does with France.
The attitude of assuming that your own ways of doing things are best, no matter where or under what conditions they are applied.

Lecture 2: A cultural profile that develops tentative expectations, some cultural context, as a backdrop to managing in a specific international setting. Lecture 3: Assuming that every member of a society or subculture has the same characteristics. Astute managers deal with people as individuals.

Lecture 2: Hall's term for the amount of space people feel they must set between themselves and others. Zones: intimate 0.45 m, personal 1.2 m, social 3.6 m, public 7.6 m. Lecture 3: The influence of proximity and space on communication: both personal space and office space or layout.
High context: not just the message matters, relation oriented, information implicitly received. Low context: explicit messages, task oriented, information explicitly conveyed.
Monochronic people do one thing at a time and stick to plans. Polychronic people do many things at once, change plans easily and put people first.
Lewis's three categories: linear-active (plans step by step, sticks to facts), multi-active (emotional, people-oriented), reactive (listens, never confronts, must not lose face).
A society's acceptance of unequal power distribution. High: authority and hierarchy respected, autocratic leaders. Low: superiors and subordinates see one another as equals.
How far people feel threatened by ambiguous situations. High: strict laws, closely followed procedures, low-risk decisions. Low: comfortable with ambiguity, more risks, more job mobility.
Individualism: looking after yourself and your immediate family only. Collectivism: tight social frameworks, emotional dependence on the organization, strong belief in group decisions.
Masculinity: assertiveness, materialism, lack of concern for others prevail. Femininity: concern for others, relationships and quality of life.
Keeping links with the past while facing the present and future. Low scorers are normative (traditions, suspicious of change). High scorers are pragmatic (modern education).
The extent to which people try to control desires and impulses. Relatively weak control is Indulgence. Relatively strong control is Restraint.
Universalistic cultures apply rules and systems objectively, whatever the circumstances. Particularistic cultures stress relationships and apply rules more subjectively.
Trompenaars: affective or emotional cultures express emotions openly. Neutral cultures do not.
Specific: work and private life kept apart. Diffuse: work spills over into personal life. Achievement: status from personal results. Ascription: status from class, age, gender.
Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness Research Program, founded in 1991 by Robert J. House (Wharton). It uses questionnaires and focuses on leadership behavior.
The sender encodes meaning into a message. The receiver decodes the meaning. The medium carries the message between them.
What disturbs a message across cultures. The decoder's culture becomes part of the meaning when he or she interprets the message sent by the encoder.
The process in which people look for an explanation of another person's behavior.
A particular source of noise in communication. They are one of the attitudes that underlie behavior, communication and interpretation.
People who make communication personal by showing emotions openly or using emotional appeals to persuade. Examples: Russia, Hungary, Poland.
People who put emphasis on the content of the communication, not personal expression. Examples: Slovenia, Lithuania, Czech Republic.
Communication through body movements. Oculesics (eye behavior) is the slide's example.
How something is said rather than the content: rate of speech, tone and inflection of voice, other noises, laughing, yawning and silence.
Also called material culture: the way we communicate through material artifacts.

High-contact cultures stand close and touch a lot (South America, Arabs, South Europe). Low-contact cultures have a distant body language style (North America, Asia, North Europe). Haptic means touching.
Time is experienced as linear: spent, saved, made up or wasted. People do one thing at a time. Examples: Switzerland, Germany, United States.
Time is nonlinear. People tolerate many things at once and stress involvement with people. Examples: Latin Americans, Arabs.
Feelings and thoughts are not said openly. You read between the lines, and style is indirect. Examples: Asia, Middle East, Africa, Mediterranean.
Feelings and thoughts are put into words and information is explicit. Style is straight. Examples: Germany, Switzerland, US, Scandinavia.
The Japanese communication style that emphasizes saving and giving face, reciprocity, and an underlying distrust of words and analytic logic.
Japanese information and decision system in which decision making is consensual.
