quiz.q: What is CSR, according to the lecture?
options: A company obeying only the laws of its home country
A government forcing firms to report their social impact
A company regulating itself voluntarily, going beyond the legal minimum
The decisions and interactions of individual employees
quiz.why: Slide 6 defines CSR as voluntary self-regulation beyond the legal minimum. The last option is the slide's definition of ethics, not CSR.

quiz.q: In which year did the UN draft its first CSR guidelines for multinational corporations?
quiz.why: Slide 6 gives 2003. 1992 is the Rio conference (slide 44) and 2015 is the 2030 Agenda (slide 45).

quiz.q: How do CSR decisions differ from ethics, according to slide 6?
options: They are made only by individual employees
They are required by law in every country
They affect fewer people but are more personal
They are made at a higher level and affect far more people
quiz.why: Slide 6: ethics is decisions of individuals, while CSR decisions are bigger. The first wrong option describes ethics.

quiz.q: A manager applies her home country's morality in the host country, whatever the local system of ethics. Which approach is this?
quiz.why: Slide 13: the ethnocentric approach applies home-country morality regardless of the host system. Ethical relativism is the opposite, adopting the local code.

quiz.q: A firm adopts the local moral code of whatever country it operates in. Which approach is this?
quiz.why: Slide 13 defines ethical relativism as adopting the local moral code. The ethnocentric approach keeps the home-country code.

quiz.q: Which of the three approaches on slide 13 is marked “preferable”?
quiz.why: Slide 13 marks moral universalism as preferable and ethical relativism as “conflict”.

quiz.q: What does the Del Monte example in Kenya show?
options: Pineapple farms bring export earnings but take up scarce farmland
Stitching soccer balls forces a choice between living wages and child labour
Pesticides banned at home come back as imported food
Paying mail carriers keeps goods moving
quiz.why: Slide 10: Del Monte brings export earnings but takes scarce farmland. The soccer ball case is the separate Pakistan example on the same slide.

quiz.q: Which describes the EU approach to business ethics on slide 11?
options: Clear, universal rules: treat everyone by the same standard
Profit is the only goal of the firm
Broader social aims: environment, shared values, relationships
Business norms have fully converged with the US
quiz.why: Slide 11 gives the EU broader social aims. Clear universal rules are the US approach.

quiz.q: Which is one of the three ways to deal with confusion about cross-cultural dilemmas?
options: Entering markets by buying existing firms
Letting each subsidiary set its own rules
Adjusting reward systems to reflect the company's commitment to CSR
quiz.why: Slide 12 lists dialog with stakeholders, principles and procedures, and adjusted reward systems. The first two wrong options are criticisms of MNCs from slides 35 and 36.

quiz.q: Which code was formerly called the Electronic Industry Code of Conduct?
quiz.why: Slide 14: the Responsible Business Alliance was formerly the Electronic Industry Code of Conduct. The Sweatshop Code is a separate Clinton-era code.

quiz.q: Which code is an ISO-style, certifiable labour standard?
quiz.why: Slide 14 describes SA8000 as an ISO-style, certifiable labour standard. The Responsible Business Alliance is an industry self-regulating, with supplier audits.

quiz.q: Which is one of the four areas of the UN Global Compact principles?
quiz.why: Slide 15: human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. Consumer protection is an area of the international codes on slide 18, not of the Global Compact.

quiz.q: Who is named on the slides for the integrated international codes of conduct (ICC, OECD, ILO, UN)?
quiz.why: Slide 17 is titled Getz's integrated International Codes of Conduct. Robertson and Crittenden belong to the moral philosophy exhibit on slide 29.

quiz.q: Which is one of the five sources in Getz's integrated codes?
options: The OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises
quiz.why: Slide 17 lists the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. The Anti-Bribery Convention is a different OECD document, on slide 32.

quiz.q: Under which of the three code areas does “environmental protection” belong?
quiz.why: Slide 18 puts technology transfer and environmental protection under MNC and Public. MNC and Owners is not an area on the slide.

quiz.q: Which expectation is listed under employment practices?
options: Use local resources and personnel for R&D
Refrain from improper involvement in local politics
Give advance notice of plant closures and mitigate effects
quiz.why: Slide 25 lists advance notice of plant closures. Local equity participation is under economic policy (slide 19), and local R&D is under technology transfer (slide 22).

quiz.q: Which expectation is listed under economic and development policies for MNC and host government?
options: Provide proper labelling and accurate advertising
Refrain from interfering in intergovernmental relations
quiz.why: Slide 19 includes reinvesting profits in host countries. Information on environmental impacts is under environmental protection (slide 23).

quiz.q: Which is listed as an attraction of doing business in China?
options: The largest economy in the world
quiz.why: Slide 26 lists a skilled workforce, 1.4B consumers, an EV and green-tech hub, and the 2nd-largest economy. China is not called the largest economy.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between gift-giving and bribery on slide 31?
options: Gift-giving is illegal everywhere; bribery is legal in some cultures
Gift-giving needs a formal complaint; bribery does not
Gift-giving is paid in cash; bribery is paid in goods
Gift-giving is open; bribery is secret and transactional
quiz.why: Slide 31 states that gift-giving is open and bribery is secret and transactional. Bribery of officials is illegal everywhere.

quiz.q: Which law bans bribing foreign officials to win business, with heavy fines and prison?
options: The FCPA (US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act)
quiz.why: Slide 32 describes the FCPA this way. The OECD convention is an agreement signed by countries and is hard to enforce without a formal complaint.

quiz.q: What does the 2025 FCPA update on slide 32 remind us of?
options: The OECD convention replaced the FCPA
Even “universal” rules can shift with politics
Bribery is legal when tied to cartels
quiz.why: Slide 32: enforcement was paused from February to June 2025, then reopened by the DOJ. It was paused, not repealed.

quiz.q: Which country has the highest score (least corrupt) on the 2025 CPI slide?
quiz.why: Slide 33 lists Denmark with 89. Finland is next with 88.

quiz.q: Which country has the lowest score (most corrupt) on the 2025 CPI slide?
quiz.why: Slide 33 lists South Sudan with 8. Somalia is next with 9.

quiz.q: What score does Lithuania have on the 2025 CPI, according to slide 33?
quiz.why: Slide 33: Lithuania scores 65 (rank 28). 64 is the US score (rank 29).

quiz.q: What should an MNC do, according to slide 34, if ethical problems cannot be resolved?
options: Ask the host government to change its law
quiz.why: Slide 34 lists withdrawal from that market as the last policy. Matching local practice is the risk side of the dilemma on slide 31.

quiz.q: Which is a common criticism of MNC subsidiary activities?
options: R&D stays at headquarters, limiting genuine technology transfer
They share ownership equally with local people
They lower interest rates for domestic firms
They reserve junior roles for expatriates
quiz.why: Slide 36, criticism 5. On slide 35, MNCs raise interest rates and reserve senior (not junior) roles for expatriates.

quiz.q: A host country partly or fully closes its borders, using tariff and nontariff barriers, to withstand foreign products. Which concept is this?
quiz.why: Slide 40 defines protectionism this way. Nationalism is public opinion against foreign influences, with no border measures.

quiz.q: What are the three pillars of the “Triple Bottom Line”?
quiz.why: Slide 43 gives Economic + Social + Environmental.

quiz.q: Which author argued that the great divisions among humankind will be cultural, and called this the clash of civilizations?
quiz.why: Huntington wrote The Clash of Civilizations (s6). Hall wrote on proxemics and context, and Schein on culture levels, not on conflict between civilizations.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six characteristics of culture on the slides?
quiz.why: The six are learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned and adaptive (s10). Competitive is not among them.

quiz.q: Which level of Schein's model is deeply embedded, self-evident and unconscious, and hard to recognize from within?
quiz.why: The deepest level is the basic underlying assumptions (s14, s16). Espoused values are the standards and rules an organization makes public.

quiz.q: A manager shows awareness of and honest caring about another individual's culture. Which concept is this?
quiz.why: The slide defines cultural sensitivity, or cultural empathy, as awareness plus honest caring (s17). Stereotyping is a tentative profile, not caring.

quiz.q: In the Saudi opening profile, about what share of the total workforce is still foreign-born?
quiz.why: The slide says about 77 percent is foreign-born (s5). 35 percent is women's share of the workforce, and 17 percent was their share in 2017.

quiz.q: Individual management styles shift to become similar to one another, through industrialization and worldwide coordination. What is this called?
quiz.why: Convergence is the shifting of management styles to become similar (s18, s21). Contingency management means adapting to the local environment (s26).

quiz.q: What is the subconscious reference point of one's own cultural values called?
quiz.why: The self-reference criterion is the subconscious reference point of one's own cultural values (s21). Espoused values are a Schein level.

quiz.q: A Frenchman expects people from another country to fall automatically into patterns of behavior common in France. Which term does the slide use?
quiz.why: The slide gives this as the example of parochialism (s21). Ethnocentrism is the attitude that your own ways are best, which the example does not say.

quiz.q: A Camay soap commercial (P&G, US) backfired in Japan. Which attitude does the slide link to this example?
quiz.why: The slide places the Camay example under ethnocentrism: Japanese viewers saw the man's behavior as bad manners (s21). Cultural sensitivity is awareness and caring about another culture, which the example does not show.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven cultural subsystems?
quiz.why: The seven are kinship, education, economic, political, religion, health and recreation (s24-25). Language is not a subsystem on the slides.

quiz.q: On the GLOBE results table (slide 71), which two countries have the highest power distance?
quiz.why: Slide 71 lists Russia and Spain as highest on power distance. Denmark and Netherlands are the lowest, and England and France are in the medium group. Austria and Denmark are highest on uncertainty avoidance.

quiz.q: In Hall's proxemics zones, which space reaches up to 3.6 m (12 ft)?
quiz.why: Social space reaches 3.6 m. Personal space reaches 1.2 m, intimate space 0.45 m and public space 7.6 m (s30).

quiz.q: Which group is ranked as the most high-context on the slide?
quiz.why: The ranking from most high-context starts with Japanese, then Arabic (s32). English and German come further down.

quiz.q: People change plans often and easily, borrow and lend things often, and build lifetime relationships. Which kind of people is this?
quiz.why: These are the polychronic traits (s33). Monochronic people adhere religiously to plans and seldom borrow or lend.

quiz.q: In Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck's model, which answer belongs to the question about the temporal focus of human activity?
quiz.why: Temporal focus has future, present and past (s36). Doing belongs to modality of activity and Dominant to relationship to nature.

quiz.q: A culture listens most of the time, never confronts, must not lose face and treats statements as promises. Which Lewis category is this?
quiz.why: These are Lewis' reactive traits (s38). Linear-active talks half the time and confronts with logic.

quiz.q: On Lewis' triangle, which pair of countries sits at the linear-active corner?
quiz.why: Germany and Switzerland are at the linear-active corner (s39). U.S.A. and the Netherlands lie on the side between linear-active and multi-active.

quiz.q: Which Schwartz value type did English speaking countries value highly?
quiz.why: English speaking countries highly valued Mastery and had higher values on Hierarchy than on Egalitarianism (s42). Embeddedness dominated the Middle East and most of Asia.

quiz.q: Which pair is one of the four features Gesteland uses for his cultural groups?
quiz.why: Gesteland uses deal or relationship focus, formal or unformal, polychronic or monochronic, and reserved or expressive (s40). The other pairs are Trompenaars' (s59).

quiz.q: Hofstede's research is based on how many people in how many countries?
quiz.why: The slide says 116,000 people in 50 countries, all in one firm, IBM (s45).

quiz.q: Formal authority and hierarchy are very respected, and leadership tends to be autocratic and centralized. Which Hofstede result is this?
quiz.why: This is the slide's description of high power distance cultures (s47). High uncertainty avoidance is about strict laws and low-risk decisions.

quiz.q: Which description matches collectivism in Hofstede's model?
options: Looking after yourself and your immediate family only
Weak control of desires and impulses
Tight social frameworks and strong belief in group decisions
quiz.why: Collectivism entails tight social frameworks, emotional dependence on the organization and strong belief in group decisions (s51). The first distractor is individualism.

quiz.q: According to the slide, what tends to be found in more feminine cultures?
quiz.why: More feminine cultures have less work-family conflict, less job stress, more women in high-level jobs and a reduced need for assertiveness (s51).

quiz.q: Which approach do societies that score high on long-term orientation take?
options: Normative: they prefer time-honoured traditions and view change with suspicion
Restrained: they control desires and impulses strongly
Pragmatic: they encourage modern education to prepare for the future
Hierarchical: they accept unequal power distribution
quiz.why: High scorers are pragmatic (s55). The normative approach describes low scorers on long-term orientation.

quiz.q: In Hofstede's wording, what is relatively weak control of desires and impulses called?
quiz.why: Relatively weak control is Indulgence and relatively strong control is Restraint (s55).

quiz.q: On the Hofstede Insights chart (slide 58), which of the four countries has the lowest masculinity score?
quiz.why: Lithuania scores 19 on masculinity. China is 66, Japan 95 and US 62 (s58).

quiz.q: Which cultures apply rules and systems objectively, without consideration of individual circumstances?
quiz.why: Universalistic cultures apply rules objectively (s60). Particularistic cultures stress relationships and apply rules more subjectively.

quiz.q: In which kind of culture do status and influence come from class, age and gender?
quiz.why: In ascription-oriented cultures status comes from society: class, age, gender (s62). In achievement-oriented cultures it comes from personal achievement.

quiz.q: In which kind of culture do people compartmentalize their work and private lives, and tend to be more open and direct?
quiz.why: The slide says people in specific cultures compartmentalize work and private life (s62). In diffuse cultures work spills over into personal relationships.

quiz.q: Who founded the GLOBE project in 1991?
quiz.why: GLOBE was founded in 1991 by Robert J. House of Wharton (s64). Hofstede's research was done at IBM.

quiz.q: Which two countries are low on GLOBE performance orientation?
quiz.why: Russia and Argentina are low on performance orientation on both country slides (s69, s71). Sweden and New Zealand are low on assertiveness, and Germany and Spain are low on humane orientation.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the ten GLOBE geographic culture clusters?
quiz.why: Nordic Europe is one of the ten clusters (s73). The other three names are not on the slide.

quiz.q: Which concept stands for peace and harmony in the Japanese workplace on the comparative management slide?
quiz.why: The slide gives Japan as wa, peace and harmony (s78). Guanxi belongs to the Chinese family business slide (s81).

quiz.q: On the Saudi Arabia slide, what do honor and shame lead to?
options: A preference for rules and order
quiz.why: Honor and shame lead to conflict avoidance and positive reinforcement (s80). Close friendships lead to person-orientation and Theory Y, and tribalism to paternalism and nepotism.

quiz.q: On the Trompenaars obligation row (universalistic to particularistic), which country stands at the particularistic end?
quiz.why: The row runs US, GER, SWE, UK, IT, FRA, JPN, SPA, SIN, so SIN is at the particularistic end (s61). US, GER and SWE are at the universalistic end.

quiz.q: Which authors wrote Variations in Value Orientations (1961)?
quiz.why: Variations in Value Orientations (1961) is by Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck (s27, s34). Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner wrote Riding the Waves of Culture.

quiz.q: In the communication process (Exhibit 4-1), who encodes the meaning?
quiz.why: The sender encodes meaning and the receiver decodes it (s5). The medium only carries the message.

quiz.q: In the communication process exhibit, what is the source that feeds the noise?
quiz.why: Exhibit 4-1 (s5) shows culture as the source that feeds the noise. Feedback only runs from the receiver back to the sender.

quiz.q: Which definition fits attribution?
options: Looking for an explanation of another person's behavior
Assuming every member of a society has the same characteristics
quiz.why: Attribution is the process of looking for an explanation of another person's behavior (s7). The second option is stereotyping (s15).

quiz.q: A Greek employee answers 'I don't know. How long should it take?' What does the American conclude (s6)?
options: He is the boss. Why doesn't he tell me?
quiz.why: On s6 the American attributes the Greek answer to refusing to take responsibility. 'I asked for an order' is the Greek's own attribution.

quiz.q: A manager assumes that every member of a subculture has the same characteristics. Which concept is this?
quiz.why: Stereotyping is assuming that every member of a society or subculture has the same characteristics (s15). Attribution is looking for an explanation of behavior (s7).

quiz.q: What did the World Values Survey study on trust (s9)?
quiz.why: The WVS studied 90,000 people in 45 societies (s9). The other options swap or change the numbers.

quiz.q: Which group rated highest on believing that most people can be trusted (WVS, s9)?
quiz.why: Nordic countries rated highest (s9). Brazil, Turkey, Romania, Slovenia and Latvia had the lowest trust.

quiz.q: The Japanese ningensei style of communication emphasizes what (s39)?
options: Public disagreement to reach the truth
Saving and giving face, and reciprocity
Written letters that build up to the point
quiz.why: Ningensei emphasizes saving and giving face, reciprocity and distrust of words (s39). Public disagreement is avoided, and written letters are the French style.

quiz.q: How does the GLOBE slide advise communicating with people high on performance orientation (US, Switzerland, Germany)?
options: Present objective information directly and explicitly
quiz.why: High performance orientation calls for direct, explicit, objective information (s11-12). Indirect is for low performance orientation (Russia, Greece, Portugal).

quiz.q: In South America decision-making tends to be centralized. Which way does information flow (s38)?
options: From staff up to the manager
quiz.why: Centralized decision-making means information flows from the manager downward (s38). The US is the one where staff information flows to the manager, because managers delegate.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the cultural variables listed on s13?
quiz.why: The s13 list: attitudes, social organization, thought patterns, roles, language, non verbal communication, time. Leadership style is not on it.

quiz.q: A Canadian in Thailand thought double lines on the road meant 'no passing'. Which cultural variable is this?
quiz.why: The slide uses this case for thought patterns: the logical progression of reasoning varies across cultures (s15). It is not about attitudes or social organization.

quiz.q: Which step of managing cross-cultural communication says to avoid slang, idioms and regional sayings?
quiz.why: Careful encoding (s41) says to use words, pictures and gestures and avoid slang, idioms and regional sayings. Decoding is about feedback.

quiz.q: When many Asians say 'yes', what does it often mean (s17)?
options: They have heard you and are too polite to disagree
They need more time to decide
quiz.why: The slide says 'yes' often means only that they have heard you and are too polite to disagree (s17). It does not mean agreement.

quiz.q: Which countries does s19 give as examples of expressive communicators?
quiz.why: Expressive communicators: Russia, Hungary, Poland (s19). Slovenia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic are the instrumental examples.

quiz.q: Which item does s44 list under resilience?
quiz.why: Resilience: internal locus of control, persistence, tolerance for ambiguity, resourcefulness (s44). Open-mindedness and extrovertedness belong to openness.

quiz.q: Which term means communication through body movements?
quiz.why: Kinesic behavior is communication through body movements, for example oculesics (s21). Proxemics is about proximity and space.

quiz.q: Which is an example of paralanguage given on s26?
quiz.why: Paralanguage is how something is said, such as tone and inflection of voice, laughing, yawning and silence (s26). Office layout and personal space are proxemics.

quiz.q: How long do the Chinese tend to spend thinking before they speak (s26)?
quiz.why: The Chinese tend to spend about 30 seconds thinking (s26). Ten to fifteen seconds is what Americans are comfortable with.

quiz.q: Which group does s25 give as high-contact cultures?
quiz.why: High-contact: South America, Arabs, South Europe (s25). North America, Asia and North Europe are low-contact.

quiz.q: English is used on about 50% of websites. What share of internet users speaks it (s40)?
quiz.why: Only about 1 in 4 internet users speaks English (s40), so local languages drive growth. The 50% figure is for websites, not for users.

quiz.q: Which countries does s27 name as monochronic?
quiz.why: Monochronic: Switzerland, Germany, United States (s27). Latin Americans and Arabs are the polychronic examples.

quiz.q: In one culture people tolerate many things at once, change plans often and put relationships above material things. Which type is this?
quiz.why: These are polychronic traits (s28). Monochronic cultures do one thing at a time and see time as linear.

quiz.q: In which type of culture does one have to read between the lines (s30)?
quiz.why: In high-context cultures feelings and thoughts are not explicit, so you read between the lines (s30). Low-context cultures put thoughts in words.

quiz.q: Germans expect detailed information before a business decision. What do Arabs base decisions on more (s30)?
quiz.why: Arabs base decisions more on knowledge of the people involved (s30). Detailed information is the German expectation.

quiz.q: On the context chart (Exhibit 4-4, s31), which culture sits at the high-context (implicit) end?
quiz.why: The chart runs from Japan (high context) to Switzerland (low context). Germany, Scandinavia and Switzerland are at the explicit end.

quiz.q: Why does the slide say it is inappropriate to place deadlines on activities with Arabs (s35)?
options: They treat time as linear and scarce
They are polychronic and believe things happen if Allah wills
They avoid business talk in meetings
quiz.why: Arabs are polychronic and believe something will happen only if Allah wills it (s35). Linear time is the monochronic view.

quiz.q: Which is a suggestion for doing business with Arabs (s36)?
options: Set firm deadlines at the first meeting
Voice doubts and criticism in front of the group
Keep meetings short and on schedule
Avoid expressing doubts and criticism when others are present
quiz.why: The slide says to avoid expressing doubts and criticism when others are present (s36). Firm deadlines and tight schedules go against the polychronic style.

questions.q: Define CSR and explain how it differs from ethics.
questions.answer: CSR is a company regulating itself voluntarily, going beyond the legal minimum. It means actively monitoring your own compliance with laws, ethics and social norms. Ethics, in this lecture, is the decisions and interactions of individuals. CSR decisions are bigger: they are made at a higher level and affect far more people. CSR weighs the benefit against the harm MNCs create, especially in developing countries. The big question is how much a firm should care about the social effects of its decisions. In 2003 the UN drafted its first CSR guidelines for multinational corporations.

questions.q: A company must choose a code of ethics for a subsidiary abroad where local practice differs from home. Explain the three approaches and say which one the lecture prefers.
questions.answer: The lecture gives three approaches for a code of morality and ethics. Moral universalism addresses the need for a moral standard accepted by all cultures, and the slide marks it preferable. The ethnocentric approach applies the morality of the home country, regardless of the host country's system of ethics. Ethical relativism adopts the local moral code of whatever country the firm operates in, and the slide marks it conflict. For the subsidiary, the company should aim for a standard accepted by all cultures, not just copy home or local rules.

questions.q: What is the UN Global Compact? Explain its aims and its areas of principles.
questions.answer: The UN Global Compact aims to mobilize a global movement of sustainable companies and stakeholders to create a sustainable world. It supports companies to do business responsibly by aligning their strategies and operations with 10 Principles on four areas: human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. It also asks companies to take strategic actions to advance the SDGs, with an emphasis on collaboration and innovation. The bullets cover human rights, collective bargaining, the elimination of forced labour, the abolition of child labour, non-discrimination in employment, environmental responsibility and work against corruption. In 2025 it had 23,000+ business participants in 160+ countries.

questions.q: A manager works in a country where small payments to officials are normal. Use the lecture to explain the dilemma and what the company can do.
questions.answer: Questionable payments are political payments, extortion, bribes or grease money to speed up routine transactions. In some cultures bribery is normal and gift-giving is common. The key difference is that gift-giving is open, while bribery is secret and transactional. Bribery of officials is illegal everywhere, so the manager must choose between sticking to their own standard and risking lost business, or matching local practice and risking the law. The US FCPA bans bribing foreign officials. The company can develop a worldwide code of ethics, build ethical policies into strategy, assess its ethical posture regularly, and withdraw from the market if problems cannot be resolved.

questions.q: List and explain the common criticisms of MNC subsidiary activities.
questions.answer: There are nine common criticisms. One: MNCs raise capital locally, which can push up interest rates for domestic firms. Two: subsidiaries are mostly owned by the parent, so host-country people have little control. Three: senior managerial and technical roles go to expatriates, slowing local talent development. Four: technology is not always adapted to local conditions. Five: R&D stays at headquarters, limiting technology transfer. Six: they can fuel demand for luxury goods over essential goods. Seven: they often enter by buying an existing firm. Eight: they can dominate whole industries, raising demand for scarce resources and inflation. Nine: they answer only to home-country shareholders and government.

questions.q: Explain sustainability, sustainable development and the 2030 Agenda.
questions.answer: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without compromising tomorrow's resources. Its three pillars, the Triple Bottom Line, are economic, social and environmental. It also includes future generations, biodiversity, human rights, transparency and education. Sustainable development became the main guiding principle after the Rio conference of 1992. It meets the needs of the current generation without compromising future generations, and respects the limited capacity of an ecosystem to absorb human impact. In September 2015, 193 countries adopted the 2030 Agenda, with 17 SDGs and measurable targets, aiming at balanced development that leaves no one behind.

questions.q: What does the lecture recommend for MNCs operating in developing countries?
questions.answer: The lecture gives seven recommendations. MNCs should do no intentional harm, including respect for the ecosystem and consumer safety. They should produce more good than harm for the host country. They should contribute through their activity to the host country's development. They should respect the human rights of their employees. As long as local culture does not violate ethical norms, they should respect it and work with it, not against it. They should pay their fair share of taxes. They should cooperate with the local government in developing and enforcing just background institutions.

questions.q: Define culture and explain Schein's three levels.
questions.answer: Culture is acquired knowledge that people use to interpret experience and generate social behavior. It forms values, creates attitudes and influences behavior, and it is learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned and adaptive. Edgar Schein's model, also called the onion model, has three levels. Artefacts and symbols are the visible surface, such as logos, architecture, structure, processes and corporate clothing. Espoused values are the standards, values and rules of conduct an organization makes public. Basic underlying assumptions are deeply embedded, self-evident and unconscious, and hard to recognize from within. The outer layer is easy to change, and the deeper the layer, the harder it is to adjust.

questions.q: List and explain the seven cultural subsystems that influence people and their behaviour.
questions.answer: Cultural subsystems are the parts of a society through which values are communicated and passed down. Kinship guides family relationships: the nuclear family in the US, the extended family in some other countries. Education influences expectations of workers and managers' choices on recruitment, staffing, training and leadership. The economic system influences sourcing, distribution, incentives and reparation of capital. The political system imposes constraints on organizations and their freedom to do business. Religion commonly underlies moral and economic norms. The health system affects productivity, expectations and attitudes toward fitness. Recreation affects work behavior and the perception of the role of work in life.

questions.q: Explain Hall's main differences between cultures: context, proxemics and time.
questions.answer: Edward T. Hall named three important differences. Proxemics is the amount of space people feel they must set between themselves and others, with zones from intimate (0.45 m) to public (7.6 m). In low-context cultures messages are explicit and people are task oriented. In high-context cultures not just the message matters, and people are relation oriented. Japanese are the most high-context on the slide and Swiss-German the least. Monochronic people do one thing at a time and adhere to plans. Polychronic people do many things at once, change plans easily and are committed to people and human relationships.

questions.q: Describe Lewis' three cultural categories and give a country for each.
questions.answer: Richard D. Lewis (When Cultures Collide) sorts cultures into linear-active, multi-active and reactive. Linear-active people talk half the time, do one thing at a time, plan step by step, stick to facts and put truth before diplomacy. Multi-active people talk most of the time, do several things at once, are emotional and people-oriented, and put feelings before facts. Reactive people listen most of the time, never confront, must not lose face and put diplomacy over truth. On Lewis' triangle the corners are Germany and Switzerland for linear-active, Hispanic America for multi-active and Vietnam for reactive.

questions.q: Name Hofstede's six dimensions and explain how his research was done.
questions.answer: Geert Hofstede defined culture in six dimensions: power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term orientation and indulgence. Power distance is acceptance of unequal power. Individualism is looking after yourself and your close family, against collectivism. Uncertainty avoidance is feeling threatened by ambiguity. Masculinity is assertiveness and materialism, against femininity's concern for others. Long-term orientation separates normative from pragmatic societies. Indulgence is weak control of desires, against restraint. The research was based on 116,000 people in 50 countries, but all in one firm, IBM, so the results should be interpreted with caution. Example: Lithuania scores 19 on masculinity and 60 on individualism.

questions.q: Compare Trompenaars' dimensions with the GLOBE project.
questions.answer: Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner give seven dimensions: universalism vs particularism, neutral vs emotional, specific vs diffuse, achievement vs ascription, sequential vs synchronic, internal vs external control, and individualism vs collectivism. GLOBE, founded in 1991 by Robert J. House, has nine dimensions: uncertainty avoidance, power distance, social collectivism, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, assertiveness, future orientation, performance orientation and humane orientation. GLOBE results correspond generally with Hofstede and Trompenaars. It differs from Hofstede because many researchers studied many companies, while Hofstede worked alone at IBM. GLOBE also groups countries into ten clusters, such as Nordic Europe.

questions.q: Case: Bill Nugent, a Dallas developer, waits until nearly 3:45 pm for a 2:30 pm meeting in Riyadh and meets small talk. How would you help Bill?
questions.answer: Bill is judging Saudi Arabia with his own cultural reference point, the self-reference criterion (s21). Americans see time as money and keep schedules strictly (s76). Saudi culture works differently. Polychronic people change plans easily and put people and relationships first (s33), so the delay and the other men in the room are normal. Arabic is high-context on Hall's ranking, so communication is relation oriented (s31-32). Close friendships lead to person-orientation (s80), so small talk builds trust before business. I would advise Bill to plan extra time, accept the waiting and the other people present, invest in the relationship, and raise business later.

questions.q: Case: Tom Forrest, a US executive, defends a joint venture plan in a meeting in Japan after the retired president criticises it. The firm ends the talks. How would you help Tom understand?
questions.answer: Japan is a reactive culture in Lewis' terms: people must not lose face, never confront and put diplomacy over truth (s38). The slide on Japan adds wa, peace and harmony, consensus and duty, and open expression and conflict are discouraged (s78). The critic was the president's 82-year-old grandfather, who had just retired (s84). Mr. Hayakawa's silence fits this: openly contradicting the elder would break harmony. Tom's strong public defence did exactly that and caused loss of face, so the firm ended the negotiations. Tom should avoid open argument, raise concerns indirectly or in private, and work for consensus.

questions.q: Case: Fred Wagner, an American who speaks German, opens his Frankfurt presentation with humorous anecdotes, and the German firm declines his products. What went wrong?
questions.answer: Fred read the situation through his own culture. Germans prefer rules and order, and dislike inefficiency (s78). Germany is among the low-context cultures on Hall's ranking, so messages are explicit and people are task oriented (s31-32). Lewis' linear-active style sticks to facts and puts truth before diplomacy (s38). Jokes at the start of a business presentation read as not serious, so the executives doubted him despite his good German and correct greeting. Fred should have been formal, punctual and fact-based, and opened with the business case.

questions.q: Explain the communication process and cultural noise. Use the Greek and American example from the lecture.
questions.answer: In the communication process the sender encodes meaning, the medium carries the message, and the receiver decodes the meaning. Noise acts on all three, culture is the source that feeds the noise, and feedback runs from the receiver back to the sender. Cultural noise arises because the decoder's culture becomes part of the meaning. People then use attribution, looking for an explanation of the other person's behavior, and often blame confusion on the other's 'stupidity or craziness'. Example: an American asks, 'How long will it take to finish this report?' to invite participation. The Greek expects an order from the boss and answers, 'I don't know. How long should it take?' The American concludes that he refuses to take responsibility.

questions.q: Why is trust important for effective communication, and how can it be cultivated?
questions.answer: Effective communication depends on informal understandings among the parties, and these are based on trust. When trust exists, there is implicit understanding, cultural differences may be overlooked, and problems are dealt with more easily. The meaning of trust and how it is developed vary across societies, and some cultures have a greater propensity to trust. The World Values Survey studied 90,000 people in 45 societies: Nordic countries rated highest, and Brazil, Turkey, Romania, Slovenia and Latvia lowest. Three guidelines for cultivating trust: create a clear and calculated basis for mutual benefit, improve predictability by resolving conflicts and keeping communication open, and develop mutual bonding through regular socializing and friendly contacts.

questions.q: List and explain the cultural variables in communication.
questions.answer: Cultural variables affect communication via a person's perceptions, and their effects are interdependent. The list has seven. Attitudes underlie behavior and interpretation, ethnocentric attitudes are a particular source of noise, and stereotyping assumes every member of a society has the same characteristics. Social organization (nation, tribe, religious sect, profession) shapes perceptions. Thought patterns differ: a Canadian in Thailand assumed double lines meant no passing. Roles differ in who decides and who is responsible. Language, spoken and written, causes problems through idioms, body language and poor translation. Non verbal communication includes kinesic behavior, paralanguage, proxemics and object language. The seventh variable is time.

questions.q: Explain the four media of nonverbal communication, with the slide examples.
questions.answer: Nonverbal communication is behavior that communicates without words. Kinesic behavior is communication through body movements, for example oculesics. Proxemics is the influence of proximity and space on communication: high-contact cultures such as South America, Arabs and South Europe stand close, while low-contact cultures such as North America, Asia and North Europe keep distance, and French executives work in the middle of subordinates. Paralanguage is how something is said: the Chinese tend to think about 30 seconds before speaking, while Americans are comfortable with only 10 to 15 seconds of silence. Object language, or material culture, is communication through material artifacts.

questions.q: Compare high-context and low-context cultures, and monochronic and polychronic cultures.
questions.answer: In high-context cultures (Asia, Middle East, Africa, Mediterranean) feelings and thoughts are not explicit, you read between the lines, and the style is indirect. In low-context cultures (Germany, Switzerland, US, Scandinavia) thoughts are put into words and the style is straight. Germans expect detailed information before a decision, while Arabs base decisions more on knowledge of the people involved. Monochronic cultures (Switzerland, Germany, United States) see time as linear, do one thing at a time and are used to short-term relationships. Polychronic cultures (Latin America, Arabs) tolerate many things at once, change plans often and put relationships over material things.

questions.q: How should a Western manager communicate with Arabs?
questions.answer: Arabs build communication on friendship, honor and hospitality. They use loud speech for dramatic effect and flowery language, they are high-contact communicators, and time is the key in the process. They tend to do business with people, not organizations, so you should not decline hospitality or criticize in front of others. Arabs are polychronic and believe something happens only if Allah wills it, so deadlines are inappropriate and interruptions should be expected. The suggestions: be patient and build relationship and trust, put relationships before the task, avoid doubts and criticism when others are present, adapt to body language norms, and expect delays and changes in plans.

questions.q: How can a manager manage cross-cultural communication successfully?
questions.answer: The slides give five steps. Develop cultural sensitivity by anticipating the meaning the receiver will get. Encode carefully with words, pictures and gestures, and avoid slang, idioms and regional sayings. Use selective transmission: build relationships, face-to-face if possible. Decode feedback carefully by asking multiple parties and improving listening and observation. Follow up through action and inaction and keep lines of communication open. Contract follow through can be hard because cultures differ on what a contract is. Openness (open-mindedness, tolerance for ambiguity, extrovertedness) and resilience (internal locus of control, persistence, tolerance for ambiguity, resourcefulness) also help.

chapters.title: From CSR to codes of conduct
paragraphs: This lecture asks what a multinational company owes to the people it affects. The opening profile shows the problem in photos. Garment workers in Bangladesh hold signs that say “I made your clothes”. Protesters outside a Primark store hold signs that say “Primark's shame” and “Never again”. The lecture is called Managing Interdependence because a company cannot serve shareholders, workers, communities and governments one after the other. It has to deal with all of them at once.

Start with the words. CSR means a company regulating itself, voluntarily, and going beyond the legal minimum. It also means actively monitoring your own compliance with laws, ethics and social norms. Ethics, in this lecture, is the decisions and interactions of individuals. CSR decisions are bigger: they are made at a higher level and affect far more people. In 2003 the UN drafted its first CSR guidelines for multinational corporations.

The slides call this a dilemma. At one extreme, profit is the MNC's only goal. At the other, MNCs should anticipate and solve social needs. Most real firms sit somewhere in between, and that position shifts under pressure. The core issues are poverty, environment, consumer rights and worker safety, and they are now mapped onto the UN's 17 SDGs.

International CSR is harder than domestic CSR, because there are more stakeholders and more conflicts of interest. The MNC sits between home-country stakeholders, such as owners, employees, customers and unions, and host-country stakeholders, such as the host government, the community and consumers. Del Monte's pineapple farms in Kenya bring export earnings but take up scarce farmland. Stitching soccer balls in Pakistan forces a choice: pay a living wage and risk hunger for families who lose the work, or keep wages low and risk child labour.

Firms and regions do not fully agree on what to do. The idea of a “Global Corporate Culture” says business norms are converging. In practice the US and Europe still diverge. The US prefers clear, universal rules and the same standard for everyone. The EU has broader social aims: environment, shared values, relationships. The 2024 Forced Labour Regulation is an example of the EU's tougher, systemic tradition. When the confusion is real, the slides offer three tools: engage stakeholders and sometimes NGOs in a dialog, set principles and procedures for hard issues, and adjust reward systems to reflect the company's commitment to CSR.

The next question is which moral standard a manager should use. There are three approaches. Moral universalism looks for a standard accepted by all cultures, and the slide marks it preferable. The ethnocentric approach applies home-country morality whatever the host country thinks. Ethical relativism adopts the local moral code wherever the firm operates, and the slide marks it “conflict”.

Where governments have not agreed on binding global rules, industry has stepped in with voluntary but reputation-critical codes. The Sweatshop Code of Conduct, from the Clinton era in the 1990s, bans forced labour and discrimination and sets minimum wage and safety rules. The Responsible Business Alliance, formerly the Electronic Industry Code of Conduct, covers a whole industry. SA8000 is a certifiable labour standard backed by Avon and Sainsbury's.

The UN Global Compact is a large UN effort, with 23,000+ business participants in 160+ countries in 2025. Its principles sit in four areas: human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. Getz combined five sources into integrated international codes, from the International Chamber of Commerce guidelines to the UN Universal Declaration for Human Rights. These codes cover three areas: MNC and host governments, MNC and public, and MNC and persons. They ask, for example, for reinvesting profits in host countries, no bribes to public servants, accurate advertising and at least basic living wages.

chapters.title: China, corruption and sustainability
paragraphs: China is the comparative case. The slides list its attractions: a skilled workforce, 1.4B consumers, an EV and green-tech hub and the 2nd-largest economy. They also list the challenges: potentially rampant violation of workers' rights, repression of free speech, and difficulty monitoring and correcting human rights violations. For a manager, China shows the whole tension: huge opportunity next to hard human-rights questions.

Ethics vary with the cultural value system of each society. Practices that are illegal in some countries are accepted ways of doing business in others. The model by Robertson and Crittenden shows why. Economic ideology and culture lead to a dominant moral philosophy, which leads to ethical or unethical societal norms, which lead to individual behavior. Moderators act on this chain: macro-level, societal and firm-specific ones.

Bribery is where the clash is sharpest. The slide “To Bribe or NOT to Bribe?” gives three cases: paying mail carriers in Mexico so they do not “lose” mail, paying $100 to get a computer picked up and not left on a rainy dock, and gift-giving to bond social ties. Questionable payments cover political payments, extortion, bribes and grease money. In some cultures bribery is normal and gifts are expected. The key difference is that gift-giving is open, while bribery is secret and transactional. Bribery of officials is illegal everywhere, so the manager must either keep to their own standard and risk losing business, or match local practice and risk the law.

Laws try to manage the problem. The US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act bans bribing foreign officials to win business, with heavy fines and prison. In 2025 enforcement was paused from February to June, and then the DOJ reopened it, now focused on bribery tied to cartels and organised crime. Even “universal” rules can shift with politics. The OECD Anti-Bribery Convention is hard to enforce without a formal complaint. The Corruption Perceptions Index, which the slide titles Global Corruption Barometer, gives a picture. Denmark scores 89, Finland 88 and Singapore 84, while South Sudan scores 8, Somalia 9 and Venezuela 10. Lithuania scores 65, rank 28.

To cope, an MNC can develop a worldwide code of ethics, build ethical policies into strategy development, and plan regular assessment of its ethical posture. If problems cannot be resolved, it should withdraw from that market. Questionable behavior can be a slippery slope. A small bribe, a matter of personal ethics, can grow over time into something truly negligent and perhaps criminal.

Host countries have a list of nine complaints about subsidiaries. MNCs raise capital locally, which can push up interest rates for domestic firms. Subsidiaries are mostly owned by the parent, so locals have little control, and senior roles go to expatriates. R&D stays at headquarters, and MNCs can dominate whole industries and answer only to home-country shareholders and government. Against this, the slide sets benefits such as outside capital, technology, infrastructure and new jobs.

Hosts can respond in three ways. Under nationalism, public opinion favours national goals and opposes foreign influences. Under protectionism, the host closes borders partly or fully with tariff and nontariff barriers. Under governmentalism, the government uses its policy-setting role to favour national interests rather than market forces. The slides also raise an ecological issue: developed countries export hazardous waste and banned chemicals. Industrial ecology answers with alternative raw materials, new recycling methods and more use of by-products.

Sustainability means meeting today's needs without compromising tomorrow's resources, and its Triple Bottom Line is economic, social and environmental. After the Rio conference of 1992, sustainable development became the main guiding principle. In September 2015, 193 countries adopted the 2030 Agenda with 17 SDGs. The lecture ends with seven recommendations for MNCs in developing countries, from doing no intentional harm to paying their fair share of taxes. The final remarks add that there is no single global standard.

chapters.title: What culture is and how it shapes organisations
paragraphs: This lecture asks why culture matters for a manager or a negotiator. It opens with Saudi Arabia, where women outnumber men in universities and now make up about 35 percent of the workforce, up from just 17 percent in 2017. About 77 percent of the total workforce is still foreign-born. It gives a first picture of one culture. Learning goal 5 asks for the same thing: a working cultural profile as an aid to expected attitudes toward work, communication and negotiations.

Next comes S. P. Huntington. He wrote that the great divisions among humankind will be cultural, not mainly ideological or economic. Nation states stay powerful, but the main conflicts will be between nations and groups of different civilizations. His map labels the Western, Orthodox, Islamic, Sinic, Hindu, Japanese, Latin American and African civilizations, plus smaller areas such as Buddhist. In his words, the fault lines between civilizations will be the battle lines of the future.

The slides then define culture. Culture is acquired knowledge that people use to interpret experience and generate social behavior, and it forms values, creates attitudes and influences behavior. It is learned, shared, transgenerational, symbolic, patterned and adaptive. Values are basic convictions about right and wrong, good and bad, important and unimportant. People learn them in the culture where they are educated, so different values can lead to different management practices.
Edgar Schein gives a way to look inside a culture. His model has three levels. Artefacts and symbols are on the surface, such as logos, architecture and corporate clothing.

Espoused values sit in the middle. Basic underlying assumptions are the deepest level, and they are experienced as self-evident and unconscious, so they are hard to recognize from within. Because the model works like an onion, the outer layer is easy to change and the deeper layers are much harder to adjust.

Organizational culture lives inside societal culture and must respond to it. KLM extended its travel benefits to any couple who formally registered as living together, which fits Dutch attitudes. McDonald's trains employees in Russia more than in the US, because Russians are less familiar with working within a capitalist system. Some people say convergence is making management styles more alike, through industrialization and worldwide coordination, but how far culture shapes processes is still debated.

Several habits get in the way of good judgement. The self-reference criterion is the subconscious use of your own cultural values as the reference point. Parochialism is a Frenchman expecting people from another country to behave as people do in France. Ethnocentrism is the attitude that your own ways are best everywhere, as when a Camay soap commercial from P&G backfired in Japan. Cultural sensitivity, or cultural empathy, points the other way: it is awareness of and honest caring about another person's culture.

Finally, the slides list seven cultural subsystems that shape behaviour: kinship, education, the economic system, the political system, religion, health and recreation. Values reach people through these subsystems and pass down through generations. Contingency management means adapting your style to the local environment. Cultural profiles give only an approximation of national character, because subcultures exist. Canada is one example, and distinct ethnic groups in China have their own customs and dialects.

chapters.title: Models that measure culture
paragraphs: Slide 27 lists the main attempts to describe and assess cultural differences: Edward Hall, Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck, Richard D. Lewis, Richard Gesteland, Geert Hofstede, Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner, Schwartz, and the GLOBE project. This chapter covers Hall, Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck, Lewis, Gesteland, Schwartz and Hofstede. Trompenaars and GLOBE come in the next chapter. Each author looks at culture from a different side, and later slides show that the models overlap.

Edward T. Hall names three big differences. The first is proxemics, the amount of space people feel they must set between themselves and others. His zones run from intimate space up to 0.45 m, personal space up to 1.2 m, social space up to 3.6 m and public space up to 7.6 m.

The second is context. Low-context cultures use explicit messages and are task oriented. High-context cultures care about more than the message and are relation oriented, and the ranking starts with Japanese, Arabic and Latin American and ends with German and Swiss-German.

The third difference is time. Monochronic people do one thing at a time, concentrate on the job, take time commitments seriously and adhere religiously to plans. Polychronic people do many things at once, are easily interrupted, change plans often and are committed to people and human relationships. Polychronic people also borrow and lend easily and tend to build lifetime relationships, while monochronic people seldom borrow or lend and are used to short-term relationships.

Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck use six orientations. The first is the nature of people: good, evil or a mixture of good and evil. The second is the relationship to nature: dominant, in harmony or subjugation. The third is the relationship to other people: lineal, collateral or individualist.
The fourth is the modality of human activity: doing, being or containing. The fifth is the temporal focus: future, present or past. The sixth is the conception of space: private, public or mixed.

Richard D. Lewis sorts cultures into three categories. Linear-active people talk half the time, do one thing at a time, plan step by step, stick to facts and put truth before diplomacy. Multi-active people talk most of the time, do several things at once, show feelings and put feelings before facts. Reactive people listen most of the time, never confront, must not lose face and put diplomacy over truth. On his triangle, Germany and Switzerland sit at the linear-active corner, Hispanic America at the multi-active corner and Vietnam at the reactive corner.

Gesteland groups cultures using four features: deal or relationship focus, formal or unformal, polychronic or monochronic, and reserved or expressive. Shalom H. Schwartz uses a circle of seven value types: Harmony, Embeddedness, Hierarchy, Mastery, Affective autonomy, Intellectual autonomy and Egalitarianism. English speaking countries highly valued Mastery, while Embeddedness and Hierarchy dominated in the Middle East and most of Asia.

Geert Hofstede asked how to quantify culture. His six dimensions are power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term orientation and indulgence, and the first four were found first. His research covered 116,000 people in 50 countries, all in one firm, IBM, so the slides ask you to read it with caution. High power distance means respected hierarchy and autocratic leaders.

High uncertainty avoidance means strict laws and low-risk decisions. Collectivism means tight social frameworks, and femininity means concern for others and quality of life. Low long-term orientation means normative societies, and weak control of desires is called Indulgence.

The slides show older score tables and a newer chart. For China, Japan, Lithuania and the US, use the chart on slide 58. Lithuania scores 42 on power distance, 60 on individualism, 19 on masculinity, 65 on uncertainty avoidance, 82 on long-term orientation and 16 on indulgence. The US scores 91 on individualism but only 26 on long-term orientation.

chapters.title: Trompenaars, GLOBE and culture in practice
paragraphs: Trompenaars and Hampden-Turner give seven dimensions, or dilemmas, of intercultural communication. Universalistic cultures apply rules objectively, while particularistic cultures stress relationships and apply rules more subjectively. Affective cultures show emotions openly, while neutral cultures do not.

People in specific cultures keep work and private life apart, while in diffuse cultures work spills over into personal relationships. In achievement-oriented cultures status comes from personal achievement, and in ascription-oriented cultures it comes from class, age and gender. The other three are sequential versus synchronic, internal versus external control, and individualism versus collectivism.

The GLOBE project is the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness Research Program. Robert J. House of Wharton founded it in 1991. It uses questionnaires to assess average values per country, focuses on leadership behavior, and separates desired from as-is preferences. Its nine dimensions are uncertainty avoidance, power distance, social collectivism, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, assertiveness, future orientation, performance orientation and humane orientation.

GLOBE results correspond generally with those of Hofstede and Trompenaars. The difference is that many researchers with varied perspectives took part, while Hofstede worked alone, and GLOBE studied many companies where Hofstede studied IBM. On the country slides, Sweden and New Zealand are low on assertiveness, Russia and Argentina are low on performance orientation and on future orientation, and Germany and Spain are low on humane orientation. GLOBE also groups countries into ten clusters, from Anglo and Latin America to Nordic Europe, Arab and Confucian Asia. Slide 74 then shows that the models overlap, with time appearing in five of the six.

The last part of the lecture moves from models to practice. Four critical value differences matter: time, change, material factors and individualism. To Americans time is money, while in Latin America the word for tomorrow means sometime in the future. Western people believe they can control the future, while many non-Western societies believe in destiny and may be passive or hostile toward change. Americans value physical goods and status symbols, and in the US the focus is on I, while in China there is more emphasis on conformity and cooperation.

The slides also look at countries. Japan is about wa, peace and harmony, with consensus and duty and with open conflict discouraged. Germany prefers rules and order and dislikes inefficiency and tardiness.

In South Korea honest criticism is rare, and in Latin America it is very important to maintain harmony and save face. In Saudi Arabia, tribalism leads to paternalism and nepotism, close friendships to person-orientation and Theory Y, and honor and shame to conflict avoidance. Chinese family businesses put people ahead of business and rely on guanxi connections.

Culture also meets the Internet. In Korea, 98 percent of homes have high-speed Internet. In Sweden and many other European countries the government closely monitors the use and sharing of consumer data, while the US collects a great deal of information. This suggests that e-commerce must take local approaches to markets, customs, languages and currencies.

Three cases close the lecture. Bill Nugent is kept waiting in Riyadh and meets small talk, which fits polychronic time and a relationship-first culture. Tom Forrest defends a plan in a Japanese meeting and breaks harmony, which fits a reactive culture and wa. Fred Wagner opens in Frankfurt with jokes, which a rule-minded, fact-based German audience reads as not serious. In each case, name the culture, apply the slide concept, and then say what the manager should do.

chapters.title: How a message travels, and where trust fits in
paragraphs: This lecture is about how people send and receive meaning across cultures. It starts with a case. Google Street View was frozen in Germany for 12 years, from 2011 to 2023, after about 244,000 households asked for their homes to be blurred. Meta was fined 1.2 billion euros in 2023 and TikTok 530 million euros in 2025. The slide says there is a big difference in the culture of privacy between the US and Europe.

The slide then says what the case shows. Communication is a critical factor in cross-cultural management issues, most of all in interpersonal ones: motivation, leadership, group interactions and negotiation. So a manager or negotiator needs to understand how a message moves from one person to another.

The communication process has three parts. The sender encodes meaning, the medium carries the message, and the receiver decodes the meaning. Noise acts on all three parts. The exhibit shows culture as the source that feeds the noise, and feedback runs from the receiver back to the sender.

Cultural noise appears when a member of one culture sends a message to a member of another. The message holds the meaning the encoder intended. But the decoder's culture becomes part of the meaning when he or she interprets it. Attribution is the process in which people look for an explanation of another person's behavior. When someone does not understand another, he or she usually blames the confusion on the other's 'stupidity or craziness'.

The Greek example makes this concrete. An American asks, 'How long will it take to finish this report?' He thinks he has asked the Greek to participate. The Greek thinks: He is the boss, so why doesn't he tell me? The Greek answers, 'I don't know. How long should it take?' and the American concludes that he refuses to take responsibility.

Effective communication depends on informal understandings among the parties, and these rest on trust. When trust exists, there is implicit understanding, cultural differences may be overlooked, and problems are dealt with more easily. The meaning of trust and how it is developed vary across societies, and some cultures are more trusting than others. The World Values Survey studied 90,000 people in 45 societies. Nordic countries rated highest, while Brazil, Turkey, Romania, Slovenia and Latvia had the lowest trust.

The slide gives three guidelines for cultivating trust. Create a clear and calculated basis for mutual benefit. Improve predictability by resolving conflicts and keeping communication open. Develop mutual bonding through regular socializing and friendly contacts.

The GLOBE project shows which style fits which culture. High performance orientation, as in the US, Switzerland and Germany, calls for direct and explicit information. Low performance orientation, as in Russia, Greece and Portugal, calls for a more indirect approach. Low assertiveness, as in Sweden, calls for a friendly, two-way approach, and high humane orientation, as in Ireland, calls for avoiding conflict and being supportive.

chapters.title: Variables, nonverbal signals, Arabs and good practice
paragraphs: Cultural variables affect communication through a person's perceptions: attitudes, social organization, thought patterns, roles, language, non verbal communication and time. Their effects are interdependent. Ethnocentric attitudes are a particular source of noise, and stereotyping means assuming that every member of a society has the same characteristics. A Canadian in Thailand assumed double lines meant no passing, just as in Canada. Language adds more noise: when many Asians say yes, it often means only that they have heard you and are too polite to disagree.

The lecture also separates expressive from instrumental communicators. Expressive ones show emotions openly, as in Russia, Hungary and Poland. Instrumental ones stress content, as in Slovenia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic. Nonverbal cues are often said to carry 65-93% of interpreted meaning, and the slide marks this as a debated estimate. The four media are kinesic behavior, proxemics, paralanguage and object language.

Proxemics is about space. Space communicates power in the US and Germany, where executives may have large corner offices, while French executives work in the middle of subordinates. High-contact cultures (South America, Arabs, South Europe) stand close and touch a lot, and low-contact cultures (North America, Asia, North Europe) keep more distance. Paralanguage is how something is said. The Chinese tend to think for about 30 seconds before speaking, while Americans are comfortable with only 10 to 15 seconds of silence.

Time works in two ways. Monochronic cultures such as Germany, Switzerland and the US see time as linear and do one thing at a time, while polychronic cultures such as Latin America and the Arabs tolerate many things at once and put involvement with people first. Context is the other big idea. In high-context cultures you read between the lines, and in low-context cultures thoughts are put into words. The chart runs from Japan at the implicit end to Switzerland at the explicit end.

Americans find the Asian poker face hard to read, because Americans stress talking and Asians stress listening. To Americans silence is a break in communication, and to Asians it is part of communication. With Arabs, communication is built on friendship, honor and hospitality. Arabs do business with people, not organizations, and they are polychronic, so deadlines are inappropriate. Be patient, put relationships first and avoid criticism in front of others.

Channels differ too. In the US information flows from staff to manager, in South America from the manager downward, and in Japanese ringi systems decisions are consensual. Japanese ningensei stresses saving and giving face, while Americans are explicit and adversarial. On the web, English is on about 50% of websites, yet only about 1 in 4 users speaks it, so e-commerce must adapt to local cultures.

To manage all this, the slides give five steps: develop cultural sensitivity, encode carefully, transmit selectively, decode feedback carefully, and follow up. Contract follow through can be hard, because cultures have different ideas about what constitutes a contract. Openness and resilience help in this work. So do the seven behaviors tied to effectiveness: respect, interactive posture, orientation to knowledge, empathy, interaction management, tolerance for ambiguity and other-oriented role behavior.

inspire.title: A very large business network
inspire.fact: The UN Global Compact has 23,000+ business participants in 160+ countries (2025, its 25th anniversary).
inspire.why: A quick number that proves the Global Compact is a major effort, useful in any answer about codes of conduct.
inspire.share: The UN Global Compact now has more than 23,000 business participants in over 160 countries.

inspire.title: Lithuania next to the US
inspire.fact: In the 2025 CPI, Lithuania scores 65 (rank 28) and the US scored 64 (rank 29, its lowest ever). The global average fell to a record-low 42.
inspire.why: It ties the lecture to where you study now, and the numbers are easy to recall.
inspire.share: Lithuania scores 65 on the corruption index, one point above the US, which fell to its lowest ever.

inspire.title: Soccer balls in Pakistan
inspire.fact: Paying a living wage risks hunger for families who lose the work, while keeping wages low risks child labour.
inspire.why: It shows why international CSR rarely has a clean answer, which is the point of slide 10.
inspire.share: With soccer balls in Pakistan, both choices carry a risk: hunger for families, or child labour.

inspire.title: Gifts are open, bribes are secret
inspire.fact: Gift-giving is open; bribery is secret and transactional. Bribery of officials is illegal everywhere, whatever the local custom.
inspire.why: One sentence that separates gift from bribe, a likely exam and class point.
inspire.share: The difference is simple: a gift is open, a bribe is secret and transactional.

inspire.title: KLM and the registered couple
inspire.fact: KLM extended its travel benefits policy to any couple who formally registered as living together, heterosexual or homosexual, married or not.
inspire.why: A clear example of organizational culture responding to societal culture (Dutch attitudes). Use it in an open question.
inspire.share: KLM changed its travel benefits to fit Dutch attitudes, so a company culture follows the society around it.

inspire.title: McDonald's trains Russians more
inspire.fact: McDonald's provides more extensive training to employees in Russia than to those in the US, because Russians are less familiar with working within a capitalist system.
inspire.why: Shows a company adapting to local culture instead of copying home practice.
inspire.share: McDonald's gives Russian staff more training than American staff, because the system itself is less familiar to them.

inspire.title: Tomorrow means someday
inspire.fact: In Latin America the word for tomorrow is used to mean sometime in the future, while to Americans time is money and schedules are strictly kept.
inspire.why: A one-line picture of the time difference. It also helps with the Bill Nugent case.
inspire.share: In Latin America tomorrow can mean sometime in the future, but for Americans time is money.

inspire.title: Power machinery and the father's way
inspire.fact: To a Chinese worker, the change to power machinery might suggest dissatisfaction with his father's way of life.
inspire.why: Memorable example of how attitudes to change differ in non-Western societies.
inspire.share: A Chinese worker may read new machines as a criticism of his father's way of life.

inspire.title: Lithuania against the US
inspire.fact: On the Hofstede Insights chart, Lithuania scores 82 on long-term orientation and the US 26. On individualism Lithuania scores 60 and the US 91.
inspire.why: A Lithuanian class will notice Lithuania in the chart. It gives you a concrete comparison to quote.
inspire.share: In Hofstede's chart Lithuania scores 82 on long-term orientation, while the US scores only 26.

inspire.title: Street View frozen for 12 years
inspire.fact: Google Street View was frozen in Germany for 12 years (2011 to 2023) after about 244,000 households asked for their homes to be blurred.
inspire.why: It is the opening case of the lecture and shows a communication clash between two privacy cultures. You can use it as an example in an open answer.
inspire.share: Germany kept Google Street View frozen for 12 years because about 244,000 households asked to be blurred.

inspire.title: Thirty seconds of silence
inspire.fact: The Chinese tend to spend about 30 seconds thinking before they speak, while Americans are only comfortable with 10 to 15 seconds of silence.
inspire.why: It gives you two numbers for paralanguage and a clear example of how silence causes offense.
inspire.share: Americans break a silence after 10 to 15 seconds, but the Chinese may be thinking for 30, so the American ends up interrupting.

inspire.title: Double lines in Thailand
inspire.fact: A Canadian in Thailand assumed that double lines on the road meant no passing, just as they do in Canada.
inspire.why: It is the slide's example for thought patterns. It shows that we cannot assume others use the same reasoning.
inspire.share: A Canadian in Thailand read double road lines as no passing, which shows how thought patterns differ.

inspire.title: Offices that show power
inspire.fact: US executives may have large, private corner offices, while French executives communicate their central position by working in the middle of subordinates.
inspire.why: It is an easy example for proxemics: the same idea of power uses space in opposite ways.
inspire.share: A US executive shows power with a private corner office, but a French executive works in the middle of the team.
